#749. An anti-aging drug may help protect the brain before Alzheimer's symptoms begin

A drug commonly used to prevent organ transplant rejection may offer an unexpected new approach to protecting people at increased risk of Alzheimer's disease. Researchers at the University of Missouri have discovered that rapamycin, a medication also studied for its effects on aging, can improve blood flow in the brains of middle-aged adults who carry a gene variant linked to Alzheimer's.

The findings could help scientists develop strategies to address Alzheimer's risk long before memory problems appear. The research also adds to the University of Missouri's growing contributions to understanding and potentially preventing the most common form of dementia.

The study was led by Ai-Ling Lin, a professor in the university's School of Medicine and an investigator at the Roy Blunt NextGen Precision Health building. Her work focuses on identifying changes in the brain that occur before Alzheimer's symptoms develop and finding ways to intervene early.

Why Brain Blood Flow Matters for Alzheimer's Risk

A major focus of Lin's research is the APOE4 gene variant, which is associated with a substantially increased risk of developing Alzheimer's disease later in life.

People who carry APOE4 can experience reduced blood flow in certain areas of the brain years before they begin having noticeable memory difficulties. Because these circulation changes can occur so early, researchers believe they could provide an important warning sign of increased Alzheimer's risk.

Lin's latest findings suggest that improving brain circulation with an existing medication may be one way to address these early changes.

"Alzheimer's tends to happen more in older people, especially for those with APOE4," Lin said. "If we can slow down aging in the brain for those people most at risk, maybe we can reduce the risk of them developing Alzheimer's disease."

Rapamycin is already used in medicine to prevent the immune system from rejecting transplanted organs and to treat certain rare conditions. However, researchers have also been investigating its potential to slow biological aging and protect the brain.

Before joining the University of Missouri, Lin conducted experiments involving mice that carried APOE4. Her earlier research showed that rapamycin could slow brain aging and increase blood flow in these animals.

Those results prompted an important question: Could rapamycin produce similar benefits in people who have a genetic predisposition to Alzheimer's but have not yet developed the disease?

To investigate, Lin studied healthy adults between the ages of 45 and 65, including people who carried APOE4 and others who did not.

All participants received a low daily dose of rapamycin for four weeks. When researchers examined the results, they found a notable difference between the two groups.

Brain blood flow improved among participants carrying APOE4, but the same benefit was not observed in those without the gene variant. This suggests that rapamycin may have particular potential for people whose genetics place them at greater risk of Alzheimer's.

Although the study did not establish whether the treatment could prevent Alzheimer's or preserve memory over time, the improved circulation offers a promising direction for future research.

Women With the Alzheimer's Risk Gene Saw the Greatest Benefits

Another intriguing finding emerged when the researchers examined differences between male and female participants.

Women carrying APOE4 experienced the largest improvements in brain blood flow following treatment. That result may be especially important because women account for nearly two-thirds of people living with Alzheimer's disease.

"We also found that females with APOE4 saw the greatest improvement in brain blood flow, which is significant given that nearly two-thirds of people with Alzheimer's are women," she said. "This research is an example of precision medicine, as we work to identify who can benefit from this drug the most."

The results highlight the potential of precision medicine, an approach that considers individual characteristics, including genetics, when determining which treatments may be most effective.

Rather than assuming that a medication will benefit everyone equally, researchers hope to identify the people most likely to respond.

Moving Alzheimer's Discoveries Toward Human Treatments

Lin, who is also a professor in the university's College of Arts and Science, credits Mizzou's collaborative research environment with helping advance discoveries like these.

At the Roy Blunt NextGen Precision Health building, scientists and medical professionals work together in the same facility. This collaboration is designed to help move promising laboratory findings into human clinical studies more quickly.

The latest results provide an encouraging starting point for investigating whether rapamycin could eventually help delay or reduce Alzheimer's risk in genetically vulnerable individuals. More research will be needed to determine whether the changes in brain blood flow lead to lasting improvements in brain health or a lower likelihood of developing the disease.

The study, "EXPRESS: Rapamycin increases cerebral blood flow and modulates metabolic, inflammatory, and microbiome profiles in healthy middle-aged APOE4 carriers: a pilot single-arm trial" was published in Journal of Cerebral Blood Flow & Metabolism.

Fast radio bursts are invisible, but a composer has turned thousands of them into sound at a Finnish cathedral, where a choir will sing along on Nov. 21.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Fast radio bursts, flashes of energy from faraway galaxies, are invisible to our eyes. However, we can now hear their melody, thanks to a composer who has turned them into sound.

Fast radio bursts, or FRBs, are among the most extreme events in the universe, releasing as much energy in a millisecond as the sun puts out in three days and briefly outshining entire galaxies. Since the first FRB was discovered in 2007, astronomers have detected thousands of them; however, exactly how these cosmic flares are launched remains poorly understood. Recent evidence points to at least one burst coming from the environment around a rotating neutron star.

Despite their power, FRBs last only a few thousandths of a second before vanishing into space. Catching one takes luck, as a telescope has to be pointed at the right patch of sky at the right moment. That changed with CHIME (the Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment) in British Columbia. With a very wide field of view and a supercomputer to process its data, CHIME more than quadrupled the number of known FRBs in its first year of operation alone. Between 2018 and 2023, CHIME recorded 4,539 bursts from 3,641 sources.

As pulses of radio waves, our eyes haven't evolved to see FRBs, nor can we hear them as they aren't sound waves. Well, not until now."Artist and composer Andrew Melchior turned all of the CHIME bursts into sound for "The Logos," an installation that has played daily at Oulu Cathedral in Finland since early April and is scheduled to run through the end of the year. Melchior and Kiyoshi Masui, an associate professor of physics at MIT, "sonified" the bursts, translating data into acoustics so that human ears can hear them.

The structure of each real signal is mapped to varying musical pitches and played through 12 loudspeakers spread throughout the cathedral. The result is a range of tones, with distant FRBs humming, rumbling, popping, and whistling.

The signals are old by any human measure. According to a description on Melchior's website, the youngest in the work are about 50 million years old, and the oldest are about 8 to 9 billion years old.

Physics also plays a role in what is heard. Each burst arrives with its high frequencies first and sweeps downward, stretched by its journey through intergalactic gas, "and you can hear that dispersion as it falls from the dome," Melchior told Space.com by email.

Since their discovery in 2007, the bursts are also still yielding discoveries. Last month, astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope pinpointed the host galaxy of the most distant FRB yet, one that went off when the universe was only about 3 billion years old. The galaxy, a small, young, star-forming dwarf, was far smaller than expected. That makes it harder to square with the theory that FRBs come from merging neutron stars, researchers say, which would take billions of years to occur.

This fits better with a second theory, in which a young, highly magnetic neutron star called a magnetar produces the burst soon after a massive star explodes, according to NASA.

Back on Earth, an upcoming event at Oulu Cathedral offers a more immediate encounter with the bursts. On Nov. 21, 30 singers will stand among the audience and "sing back to the sky in Finnish" while Melchior plays the bursts live from a keyboard, he told Space.com by email.

"The fast flashes will echo as snare-like beats bouncing through the cathedral," Masui said in a previous MIT statement.

"It should feel rich and layered, while also revealing something real about how these signals travel across billions of years of cosmic space before reaching Earth."

Sharmila Kuthunur is an independent space journalist based in Bengaluru, India. Her work has also appeared in Scientific American, Science, Astronomy and Live Science, among other publications. She holds a master's degree in journalism from Northeastern University in Boston.

#746. Scientists discover stunning new Amazon fish that may already be endangered

A tiny fish with brilliant orange markings has been discovered in the Brazilian Amazon, but scientists warn that the newly identified species may already be at risk of extinction. Found in a handful of forest pools threatened by human activity, the colorful fish has prompted researchers to call for urgent conservation measures.

The new species, named Laimosemion laranja, belongs to a group of small freshwater fish known as killifish. It measures less than three centimeters in standard length, but its appearance is anything but ordinary. Males have rows of bright orange spots along the front half of their bodies, followed by bold orange chevron patterns near the tail. These vivid markings stand out against their pale gray sides.

The discovery was made during fieldwork in the Rio Cajari drainage in southern Amapá, a state in northern Brazil. The research team included scientists from the Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Norte, Instituto Peixe das Nuvens, Universidade Federal do Pará, and University of West Florida.

A Striking Discovery in the Amazon Rainforest

The researchers were exploring how different freshwater fish in the Rivulidae family have evolved their life cycles and survival strategies across Brazil's diverse environments. During their surveys, they encountered a fish whose unusual coloration immediately stood out.

"We are developing a research project aimed at investigating the evolution of life-history strategies in freshwater fishes of the family Rivulidae across different biomes in Brazil," said lead researcher Yuri Abrantes of the Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Norte. "During our sampling in small rivers locally known as 'igarapés' in the Rio Cajari region, in Amapá State, we found this fish with a very striking coloration, which immediately caught our attention."

Although the fish looked different from known species, its appearance alone was not enough to establish that it was new to science. The team carefully examined its body proportions, counted its scales, and studied features of its skeleton. They compared these characteristics with those of closely related species and analyzed its mitochondrial DNA to determine whether it represented a distinct species.

"It was an unexpected moment," Abrantes recalled. "Initially, what most caught our attention was the impressive coloration of the males and females, which was unlike anything we had previously encountered in the study area. This sparked our admiration and a great deal of curiosity."

Genetic testing ultimately confirmed that the fish was a previously unrecognized species. For the researchers, the finding was particularly meaningful because it highlighted how much remains to be discovered in parts of the Amazon that are both poorly studied and increasingly threatened.

Once the genetic analysis confirmed the fish's distinct identity, he said, "it was something special, as we saw an opportunity to contribute to increasing our knowledge of Amazonian biodiversity and to draw attention to the conservation of areas that are still poorly explored but highly threatened."

Why Scientists Named the New Fish Laranja

The name Laimosemion laranja reflects both the fish's remarkable appearance and the place where it was discovered. In Portuguese, laranja means orange, referring to both the color and the fruit. The name also pays tribute to Laranjal do Jari, the municipality in Amapá where the species was found.

"We wanted to choose a name that would highlight a characteristic of the fish while also fostering a sense of connection with the people of the region where it was discovered," Abrantes explained.

Beyond its colorful appearance, the discovery could help scientists better understand the evolution of Amazonian killifish. Some members of this group have developed an extraordinary way to survive in habitats that periodically dry out. Their embryos can stop developing and remain dormant in damp mud, resuming development when seasonal rains refill the pools.

"Laimosemion represents one of the five independent origins of the annual life cycle within the family Rivulidae," said Abrantes. "Laimosemion laranja is particularly interesting because it expands our knowledge of the diversity and evolution of this group in the region."

Newly Discovered Amazon Fish May Already Be Endangered

Despite the excitement surrounding the discovery, the future of Laimosemion laranja is uncertain. Scientists have found it in only three small forest pools near Laranjal do Jari, and every known location shows signs of environmental disturbance.

Deforestation, mining, and urban development are putting pressure on the surrounding habitats. One of the pools is close to water that has been discolored by sediment from mining activities. Another is located within the city itself, where plastic pollution is affecting the environment.

The species' entire known range is estimated to cover just 25 square kilometers. Because its habitat is so restricted and faces multiple threats, the researchers believe the fish meets the criteria for classification as Endangered under guidelines established by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN).

To improve its chances of survival, the team has recommended expanding the boundaries of the nearby Rio Cajari Extractive Reserve to include the areas where the fish lives.

The discovery adds another species to the Amazon's remarkable biological diversity while underscoring the need to protect habitats that scientists have barely begun to explore. Without stronger conservation measures, species such as Laimosemion laranja could face serious threats before researchers have the opportunity to fully understand them.

The study was published in the open access journal Zoosystematics and Evolution.

#745. Paleontologists discover “one-in-a-million” fossil with 450-million-year-old soft tissue

A fossil dating back more than 450 million years has revealed something scientists almost never find: delicate soft tissues from an animal that lived hundreds of millions of years before dinosaurs appeared. The extraordinarily rare discovery is giving researchers a new understanding of how some of Earth's earliest marine animals lived, fed, and evolved.

The fossil belongs to an ancient crinoid, a marine animal related to modern starfish. Crinoids often resemble underwater flowers, with branching arms extending from a central body. More than 450 million years ago, these unusual creatures were among the animals thriving in Earth's earliest coral reefs, long before plants and animals had become widespread on land.

Although scientists have discovered millions of crinoid fossils, nearly all preserve only hard skeletal structures. Delicate body parts usually decay long before fossilization can occur, leaving major gaps in our understanding of how these ancient creatures functioned.

Now, paleontologists at the University of Oklahoma have identified an exceptionally rare specimen that preserves soft tissue structures, providing an extraordinary opportunity to investigate life in Earth's ancient oceans.

"After an animal dies, soft tissues like skin, eyes, or internal organs are the first things to decay," said Dr. Lena Cole, OU paleontologist and assistant curator of invertebrate paleontology at the Sam Noble Oklahoma Museum of Natural History. "Most fossils are only made up of hard parts like bones, teeth, or shells. Soft tissues are only preserved when the environment acts almost like a natural refrigerator or vacuum‑sealer -- conditions that are incredibly rare."

A 450 Million-Year-Old Fossil With Exceptionally Rare Soft Tissue

The remarkable specimen belongs to Dendrocrinus simcoensis, an extinct species of crinoid. Its preserved tube feet represent only the second known example of fossilized soft tissue in crinoids and the oldest such discovery ever documented.

Tube feet are small, flexible structures found in echinoderms, a group of marine animals that includes starfish, sea urchins, and crinoids. Because these structures are soft and easily destroyed after death, finding evidence of them in fossils is extraordinarily unusual.

"Preservation like this is truly one in a million," Cole added. "Crinoid fossils number in the millions, and this is only the second time soft tissues have ever been found."

The age of the specimen makes the discovery even more remarkable. These delicate structures have been preserved in the fossil record for nearly half a billion years, offering direct evidence of anatomy that would otherwise have disappeared.

"It's incredible these soft tissues have survived more than 450 million years," said Dr. David Wright, another OU paleontologist and assistant curator of invertebrate paleontology at the Sam Noble Oklahoma Museum of Natural History, who co‑authored the study with Cole. "For reference, these soft tissues are more than 200 million years older than the oldest dinosaur."

Ancient Feeding Structures Reveal Evolutionary Secrets

The fossil's preserved tube feet are especially valuable because they provide clues about how crinoids obtained food and interacted with their surroundings.

Unlike the teeth and jaws that many familiar animals use to eat, crinoids rely on specialized structures to capture food particles from seawater. Their tube feet play an important role in feeding and in how these animals interact with ocean currents.

The size, arrangement, and shape of these structures can differ between species, reflecting adaptations to particular habitats and feeding methods. By studying those differences, paleontologists can reconstruct aspects of an extinct animal's lifestyle, even when no living examples of that species exist.

"Since crinoid tube feet are used for feeding, you can think of them in a similar way to how we think about teeth in mammals," Wright explained. "Differences in their structure tell us about what kinds of environments a species lived in and how it fed."

Researchers also compared the ancient fossil with crinoids living in today's oceans. Those comparisons revealed notable anatomical differences, suggesting that the feeding structures of these animals have undergone substantial evolutionary changes over hundreds of millions of years.

"Comparisons with living crinoids show that the anatomy of this ancient species was very different," Cole added. "This gives us new insight into how crinoids evolved and how their feeding strategies changed over hundreds of millions of years."

A Rare Window Into Earth's Earliest Ocean Ecosystems

Beyond revealing details about one ancient species, the discovery could help scientists piece together how marine ecosystems developed during the early Paleozoic Era.

The Paleozoic was a vast chapter of Earth's history that began about 541 million years ago. During its early stages, marine environments supported an expanding variety of complex animals, while life on land was still relatively limited.

Crinoids were among the creatures that became established in early reef communities. Their fossils provide important evidence of how marine animals occupied different ecological roles and adapted to changing environmental conditions.

However, studying only living species cannot reveal the full range of forms and adaptations that existed in the distant past. Some extinct animals possessed anatomical features that have no close equivalent among their modern relatives.

"Fossilized remains of long‑extinct species can show features well outside the range of variation we see in living species," Wright said.

"By comparing ecological ways of life for extinct and modern species, we can understand how patterns of adaptive evolution have changed through time and what factors shaped the modern biosphere."

The biosphere includes all living organisms on Earth and the environments they inhabit. Understanding how it developed requires scientists to examine not only which species existed, but also how they interacted with their surroundings and one another.

Because soft tissues are so rarely preserved in ancient echinoderms, discoveries like this one provide evidence that conventional fossils cannot offer. They can help researchers identify previously unknown feeding strategies, understand ancient ecosystems, and trace evolutionary changes that eventually shaped modern marine life.

An Extraordinary Discovery Hidden in a Museum Collection

Perhaps one of the most surprising aspects of the discovery is where the fossil was found.

Although major paleontological breakthroughs are often associated with expeditions to remote locations, valuable scientific evidence can also remain unnoticed for decades in museums.

Fossil collections contain enormous numbers of specimens, many of which have never been examined by specialists with the expertise needed to recognize their most important features. As scientific knowledge and research methods improve, these collections can reveal discoveries that earlier generations overlooked.

"New fossil discoveries ultimately come from fieldwork, but museum collections play a significant role in this kind of integrative research," Wright said. "We don't always know the full significance of the specimens we collect. New technologies, ideas or expertise often find surprising ways to utilize existing specimens to make new discoveries."

The Dendrocrinus simcoensis fossil had been housed for years at Montréal's Musée de paléontologie et de l'évolution, a small museum that operates entirely with support from community donations.

Its remarkable scientific value became apparent when Cole and Wright, both specialists in crinoids, visited the museum and examined the specimen more closely.

Their investigation revealed that the fossil preserved an extraordinarily rare record of ancient soft tissue, transforming a specimen already held in a museum collection into an important source of new evolutionary evidence.

"This discovery highlights the importance of museum collections and the community support that keeps them alive," Cole said. "Without the dedication of many people caring for these collections, this research would never have been possible."

More Discoveries May Be Waiting in Museum Drawers

The finding also demonstrates why preserving and maintaining fossil collections is essential for future research.

At the Sam Noble Oklahoma Museum of Natural History, Cole and Wright oversee invertebrate paleontology collections containing more than one million specimens. Additional fossils are added every year, creating new opportunities to investigate ancient organisms and identify previously unrecognized species.

With collections of this size, no individual researcher could possibly examine every specimen in detail. A fossil that appears ordinary today might become the focus of a major discovery when studied by someone with a different specialty or new scientific tools.

Making collections available to researchers around the world increases the chances that these overlooked treasures will eventually receive the attention they deserve.

"This is why we work to make our collections accessible to researchers around the world," Wright said. "There are simply too many fossils to study over one person's career. There's more than a lifetime's worth of discoveries waiting to be found."

The extraordinary crinoid fossil is a reminder that some of the most revealing clues about Earth's distant past may already have been collected. They are simply waiting for someone to recognize what makes them special.

A long-term goal at NASA has been the ability to robotically haul back to Earth specimens from the Red Planet.

NASA is kickstarting a new initiative for its troubled Mars Sample Return (MSR) program, called the Perseverance Sample Retrieval Architecture, or PSRA in space shorthand. The plan is to establish a fresh NASA strategy for gathering Mars samples collected by the Perseverance rover and launching them back to Earth.

The PSRA initiative was noted on Nov. 9 by Tiffany Morgan, director of the NASA Mars Exploration Program (MEP), during the virtual meeting of the Mars Exploration Program Analysis Group (MEPAG).

Morgan noted that there will be a PSRA strategy team kickoff in January 2027 with a final report due in winter 2027-2028.

The backdrop to the PSRA activity is that there's one busy rover already on the Red Planet snagging and bagging samples.

NASA's Perseverance Mars rover remains on the prowl within Jezero Crater following its touchdown in February 2021. That car-sized robot has been grabbing select specimens from across the area and gingerly dropping the sealed pick-me-ups on the surface of Mars, as well as stuffing them inside the rover itself.

Those collectibles may well hold signs of past life on the enigmatic, dusty and foreboding Red Planet.

NASA and the European Space Agency have for years been intently plotting out plans to send future spacecraft to Mars and haul those Perseverance-plucked bits, pieces, and sniffs of atmosphere to Earth for rigorous inspection here on Earth using state-of-the-art equipment.

However, over the years, multiple reviews of a NASA Mars Sample Return (MSR) project by independent groups have reported sticker shock findings. Indeed, one last price tag came in at about $11 billion, with samples being returned to Earth in 2040. That finding was deemed by NASA itself as too costly and not doable within an acceptable time frame.

Yet another appraisal group ended up finding it feasible to return Mars samples as early as 2035 for a less costly ship and shoot cost of some $8 billion.

How the PSRA review deals with MSR cost and a multitude of other concerns is in the to-be-determined column.

In the first place, why are samples from Mars delivered by robotic means? Why not let a human expedition bring back the goods?

Also speaking at MEPAG was Bruce Jakosky of the Laboratory for Atmospheric and Space Physics at the University of Colorado Boulder and Department of Earth and Space Sciences at the University of Washington.

Jakosky called for an integrated approach to planning human missions to Mars. He highlighted recommendations stemming from a workshop in which he participated, held last May and organized by Explore Mars, Inc.

That report focused on the impact of MSR on reducing risk for human missions, rather than focusing on the science, Jakosky told Space.com.

"The purpose is to understand the risk to astronauts and to hardware. The risk includes that from compounds that are present in the soil that are hazardous to astronauts if breathed in," said Jakosky. "This includes perchlorates and chloromethanes that have been identified already, and detection of other species that might be present. It also includes dust that can be breathed in by astronauts and that can affect hardware wear and tear," he said.

During the MEPAG gathering, Jakosky flagged the importance of returning samples prior to human missions to Mars, such as:

Yet one more forcing factor for NASA in yet another relook at MSR is that China is making progress on its Tianwen-3 Mars Sample Return mission.

According to the China National Space Administration, the country's Tianwen-3 probe will have a lander, an ascender, a service capsule, an orbiter, and an Earth reentry module.

Tianwen-3 appears on track getting the trek underway around 2028 on two Long March-5 heavy-lift carrier rockets from the Wenchang Space Launch Site in China's southernmost island province of Hainan.

China's Tianwen-3 mission is dedicated to bring back to Earth roughly 500 grams of Red Planet collectibles in 2031.

SpaceX launched a classified mission for the U.S. Space Force from California tonight (Nov. 11), the second such flight for the company in a six-day span.

A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from California's Vandenberg Space Force Base tonight at 11:36 p.m. EST (8:36 p.m. local California time; 0136 GMT on Nov. 12), kicking off a mission called USSF-627.

Vandenberg hosted a similar liftoff less than a week ago: On Nov. 6, a Falcon 9 sent the USSF-432 mission skyward from the site, which lies on California's gorgeous but often foggy central coast.

We don't know much about USSF-627 or USSF-432; both are classified. Some experts have speculated, however, that each mission launched a batch of SpaceX's Starshield satellites for the Space Force's Space Based Sensing and Targeting portfolio, which helps the military branch track potential targets around the world.

SpaceX didn't reveal details about either USSF-627 or USSF-432, and the company ended the webcast of both launches shortly after the first stages of their Falcon 9 rockets came back to Earth.

In both cases, that touchdown occurred about 8.5 minutes after liftoff on the SpaceX droneship "Of Course I Still Love You," which was stationed downrange of Vandenberg in the Pacific Ocean.

It was the seventh mission for USSF-627's Falcon 9 booster, which carries the designation 1103.

NROL-179 | SDA-T1TL-E | SDA-T1TL-A | 3 Starlink missions

USSF-627 was the 120th Falcon 9 launch of 2026 and the rocket's 15th national-security flight of the year to date. Eighty-five of the 120 flights have been devoted to building out SpaceX's Starlink broadband constellation in low Earth orbit, which currently consists of more than 11,000 satellites.

The Falcon 9 is not on a record-breaking cadence this year. In 2025, the rocket flew a whopping 165 missions, and 122 of them were Starlink flights.

#740. A quantum breakthrough makes light behave like both a solid and a liquid

Scientists have demonstrated an extraordinary form of quantum matter that combines two properties that seem incompatible. Known as a supersolid, this unusual state has the orderly structure of a crystal while also displaying the frictionless flow associated with a special kind of liquid. Even more remarkably, researchers have now observed this behavior at room temperature, eliminating the need for the extreme cooling traditionally used to investigate such phenomena.

The breakthrough was achieved by an international team from the Faculty of Physics at the University of Warsaw, the Military University of Technology (Poland), IBM Research Zurich, and the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS). Rather than relying on atoms cooled to temperatures near absolute zero, the scientists created a supersolid using particles that combine properties of light and matter.

Published in Science Advances, the findings introduce a new way to investigate exotic quantum behavior under much more accessible conditions. They could also help advance future technologies ranging from optical computing to highly sensitive sensors.

How Can Matter Behave Like Both a Solid and a Liquid?

Under ordinary circumstances, solids and liquids behave very differently. Crystals have an organized internal structure, with their particles arranged in repeating patterns. Liquids, by comparison, can flow and change shape.

Quantum physics, however, allows matter to behave in ways that would be impossible under the familiar rules of everyday life.

One example is superfluidity, a remarkable phenomenon in which a fluid loses its viscosity, or internal resistance to flowing. A superfluid can move through extremely narrow passages without experiencing the usual friction. Imagine placing an oar into such a liquid. You would encounter almost no resistance until the oar reached a certain speed. Beyond that threshold, tiny swirling structures known as quantum vortices would suddenly form.

During the 1960s, physicists proposed an even stranger possibility. What if a superfluid could also develop the repeating internal structure normally associated with a crystal?

This hypothetical combination became known as a supersolid. In such a state, the material exhibits the spatial organization of a solid while retaining the remarkable flow properties of a superfluid.

For decades, supersolidity remained a theoretical concept. Experimental confirmation finally arrived in 2017, when researchers observed the phenomenon in ultracold atomic Bose-Einstein condensates. These condensates form when particles enter a collective quantum state and begin behaving as a coordinated system rather than as separate individuals.

The catch was that producing these conditions generally required sophisticated equipment capable of cooling matter to temperatures extremely close to absolute zero, the lowest possible temperature.

Creating a Quantum Supersolid Using Light Instead of Cold Atoms

The international TopoLight consortium approached the challenge from a different direction. Instead of using ultracold atoms, the researchers worked with unusual hybrid particles called exciton polaritons.

These quasiparticles arise when light interacts so strongly with matter that the two become coupled inside a tiny optical chamber called a microcavity. The resulting particles display characteristics of both light and matter.

Exciton polaritons are extremely short-lived, typically surviving for only a few picoseconds. A picosecond is one trillionth of a second. Despite their brief existence, these particles can organize into a Bose-Einstein condensate and collectively exhibit the behavior of a quantum superfluid.

To create the necessary conditions, the team constructed an optical microcavity containing a specially engineered liquid crystal and covered it with an organic semiconductor. The arrangement allowed light and matter to interact strongly enough to produce the desired quantum effects without the need for extreme cooling.

"Our liquid-crystal microcavities can operate even at temperatures approaching 60°C," says Professor Wiktor Piecek from the Military University of Technology, whose group developed the liquid-crystal structures.

That temperature is approximately 140°F, far above the freezing conditions normally associated with experiments involving exotic quantum matter.

Strange Patterns of Light Reveal a Supersolid

How can researchers determine whether a collection of particles has entered such an unusual state?

In this experiment, the evidence appeared in the light emitted by the sample. When the system transitioned into the supersolid phase, researchers observed a series of regularly spaced bright fringes.

These patterns indicated that the particle condensate had spontaneously developed a repeating variation in its density. This type of spatial organization is a defining feature of crystalline structures and an important sign of supersolidity.

But the researchers noticed another intriguing effect.

Each time a laser pulse excited the sample, the bright fringes appeared in a different position. Rather than following a single fixed arrangement, the quantum system repeatedly selected among several equally possible configurations.

"This is a textbook example of spontaneous symmetry breaking," explains Professor Guillaume Malpuech from Institut Pascal (CNRS). "Theory predicted that the supersolid could choose among several equivalent states, and that is exactly what we observed."

Spontaneous symmetry breaking occurs when a system that could exist in several equivalent arrangements settles into one particular configuration. In this case, the effect became visible through the changing positions of the light patterns.

The condensate also displayed another unusual characteristic called a persistent spin helix. This refers to a repeating variation in the polarization of the emitted light. Polarization describes the orientation of light's oscillating electric field.

Together, these observations revealed two different forms of order occurring at the same time. One appeared in the intensity of the emitted light, while the other appeared in its polarization.

A Difficult Experiment With Only Hours to Succeed

Achieving these results required overcoming an unexpected practical obstacle.

The organic semiconductor used in the device gradually reacted with the liquid crystal. As a result, the experimental samples had a limited useful lifetime, giving the scientists only a few hours to collect their measurements after assembly.

This restriction made careful preparation essential. The researchers needed to determine exactly which measurements to perform and in what order before beginning each experimental run.

"We had to plan the entire sequence of experiments in advance," recalls Dr. Marcin Muszyński, the paper's first author, now a postdoctoral researcher at The City College of New York. "Repeating a measurement meant fabricating an entirely new sample."

The most important measurements took place at IBM Research Zurich. There, scientists deposited thin layers of the organic semiconductor onto specialized structures designed to manipulate light. These photonic structures had been manufactured at the Military University of Technology.

The semiconductor itself was not new to the researchers. IBM scientists had investigated its quantum properties for years, including its ability to support Bose-Einstein condensation.

"We have studied the organic semiconductor MeLPPP (methyl-substituted ladder-type poly(paraphenylene) for many years and previously observed Bose-Einstein condensation in this material," says Thilo Stöferle from IBM Research. "This was the first time we combined it with a liquid-crystal microcavity."

Bringing these materials together ultimately made it possible to observe the unusual supersolid behavior at room temperature.

Why Room Temperature Quantum Matter Matters

The significance of the discovery extends beyond demonstrating another unusual phenomenon predicted by quantum physics.

Many experiments involving exotic quantum states depend on costly cryogenic systems designed to maintain temperatures close to absolute zero. These demanding conditions make research more complicated and can create substantial obstacles when scientists attempt to turn laboratory discoveries into useful technologies.

The new results show that certain exotic quantum effects can instead be investigated in photonic devices that operate at ordinary temperatures.

This could create opportunities for future technologies that use light to process information. Potential applications include ultrafast photonic devices, specialized computing accelerators inspired by the way biological brains process information, and advanced optical sensors.

The computing approach, known as neuromorphic computing, seeks to imitate aspects of the brain's information processing to perform certain tasks more efficiently. Light-based systems could eventually provide new ways to accelerate these operations.

The supersolid's exceptional sensitivity to light polarization may also prove useful for developing sensors capable of detecting extremely subtle optical changes.

These applications remain possibilities for future research, but the ability to generate the underlying quantum behavior without extreme cooling represents an important step toward making such technologies more practical.

Electrically Controlled Quantum Matter Opens New Possibilities

One of the most promising features of the experiment is that the optical device can be adjusted using electricity.

The liquid crystal microcavities provide the first electrically tunable platform for studying supersolid exciton-polariton condensates. This means researchers can alter the optical properties of the system by applying an external voltage.

Earlier experimental approaches did not offer this same degree of electrical control.

The ability to adjust the system dynamically gives physicists greater flexibility when investigating how quantum states emerge, interact, and respond to changing conditions.

It could also become valuable when designing practical quantum photonic devices, where precise control over the behavior of light and matter is essential.

By combining room-temperature operation with electrical tunability, the researchers have established a versatile platform for exploring quantum phenomena that previously required far more demanding experimental conditions.

About the University of Warsaw Faculty of Physics

The University of Warsaw has a long history of research and education in physics and astronomy. Both disciplines became part of the university in 1816, when they were included in the Faculty of Philosophy. The university subsequently established its Astronomical Observatory in 1825.

Today, the Faculty of Physics includes the Institutes of Experimental Physics, Theoretical Physics, and Geophysics, along with the Department of Mathematical Methods in Physics.

Its research encompasses nearly every major area of modern physics, from the behavior of particles at quantum scales to the structure and evolution of the universe.

The faculty employs more than 250 academic teachers and serves approximately 1,350 students and more than 150 doctoral students.

According to Shanghai's Global Ranking of Academic Subjects, the University of Warsaw ranks among the world's top 150 institutions for physics education.

#739. This AI ‘mechanic’ can peer inside the black box of other neural networks

Some AI models behave like mechanics — fixing issues in other models that they neither designed nor fully understand. Credit: Mint Images/Getty

Researchers have used an artificial-intelligence model to read and tinker with the internal workings of another AI network — offering a new way to peek into the ‘black box’ of AI.

Computer scientists usually improve models by training them in tiny increments or by building them from scratch. A team at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in Cambridge has demonstrated how an AI model called GPT-6 Astra can interpret the raw internal values of some other models well enough to predict what different parts of the systems do. It can then edit the models to make improvements — including boosting their mathematical abilities. The authors reported their findings in a preprint1 on 2 November.

ChatGPT is a black box: how AI research can break it open

ChatGPT is a black box: how AI research can break it open

Frontier AI models are “showing early sparks” of an ability to treat neural networks like files that they can read, reason about and change, says co-author Rikiya Takehi, a machine-learning researcher at MIT.

The results do not mean that Astra, developed by OpenAI in San Francisco, California, can explain or understand how a given AI network works. But the findings suggest that general-purpose AI models — such as ChatGPT or Claude — might be able to modify a network in useful ways, like a mechanic who can identify and fix issues in an engine that they neither designed nor fully understand.

Researchers already try to interpret how different components of a network create its outputs. The preprint shows that it is possible to automate some of these ‘interpretability’ methods, says Fazl Barez, an AI-safety researcher at the University of Oxford, UK.

Researchers hope that better understanding models in this way will help to create safer AI systems, although Barez cautions that this assumption is “largely untested”.

It remains unclear if Astra is going beyond applying information and techniques learned in its training. Barez says he would be surprised if Astra is able to read and interpret models in ways that go beyond existing human abilities.

Three reasons why AI is not conscious and perhaps never will be

Three reasons why AI is not conscious and perhaps never will be

Still, if developed further, such ability to reprogram models might be an asset in developing AI for science, says Marinka Zitnik, a computer scientist and bioinformatician at Harvard University in Cambridge, Massachusetts. For example, it could help to spot errors in a model ahead of real-world testing, she says.

Frontier AI systems are based on massive neural networks — brain-inspired architectures in which layers of processing units, or neurons, are linked by billions of ‘weights’, values that represent the strength of connections inside a model. The strength of each weight is slowly nudged during training to make the model better at, for example, predicting a protein structure or the next word in a sentence.

The complex way in which a model’s features link to its outputs means they are often described as black boxes. Interpretability researchers run experiments to work out, for example, which weights are activated under specific conditions. Researchers have also previously developed custom models that can learn to edit other models2.

#737. Scientists just found dinosaur blood that survived 115 million years

Scientists have discovered remarkably preserved traces of dinosaur blood inside 115-million-year-old bones, revealing that delicate biological molecules can survive far longer than previously believed. The breakthrough could transform how researchers study prehistoric animals and even influence the search for ancient life beyond Earth.

An international team led by Curtin University found fossilized red blood cells and chemical evidence of blood molecules in the remains of Aratasaurus museunacionali, a meat-eating theropod dinosaur discovered in northeastern Brazil. The findings, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, also include amino acids associated with collagen, an important structural protein found in bones and other connective tissues.

The discovery provides the first definitive chemical confirmation of molecules derived from hemoglobin inside fossilized dinosaur red blood cells. Earlier research had identified structures resembling blood cells in ancient fossils, but scientists had not conclusively demonstrated the presence of these particular molecular remains within them.

Ancient Dinosaur Blood Preserved Inside Fossilized Bones

When researchers examined the dinosaur's limb bones, they identified numerous mineralized red blood cells inside vascular canals, the tiny passages that once contained blood vessels. Chemical analysis revealed preserved heme molecules, which are components of hemoglobin, the protein that allows red blood cells to transport oxygen.

Finding these molecules provided direct chemical evidence that the fossil contained remnants of ancient blood. It also demonstrated that some biological materials once thought too fragile to survive for millions of years can remain detectable under exceptional conditions.

The study was led by John Curtin Distinguished Professor Kliti Grice, founding director of Curtin University's WA-Organic and Isotope Geochemistry Centre and an Australian Research Council Laureate Fellow.

"To detect intact heme-derived molecules in 115-million-year-old red blood cells is astonishing: this really is a landmark discovery," Professor Grice said.

"It not only extends the known fossil record of blood, but also offers a direct molecular window into the physiology of long-extinct animals so we may better understand them and the world they lived in."

How Dinosaur Blood Survived 115 Million Years

The extraordinary preservation appears to be connected to a mineral called hausmannite. This mineral helped stabilize the fossilized blood cells and preserve their molecular components (including amino acids of collagen) over an immense span of geological time.

In effect, the mineral created a natural time capsule that protected microscopic evidence of the dinosaur's biology long after its death.

Researchers believe the conditions surrounding the dinosaur's burial were also crucial. They suspect the animal was quickly covered by sediment in an environment with little oxygen and abundant microbial activity. These conditions may have helped preserve biological material that would ordinarily have broken down and disappeared.

The international research effort brought together scientists from Curtin University's School of Earth and Planetary Sciences, the Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology, the Brazilian National Museum, the Regional University of Cariri, and Johns Hopkins University.

A Discovery That Challenges Fossil Preservation Limits

The findings challenge a longstanding assumption in paleontology that molecules associated with blood, particularly those derived from hemoglobin, could not remain preserved across such enormous periods of time.

Beyond confirming the survival of ancient blood components, the discovery raises the possibility that other fossils may contain molecular information that conventional examinations have overlooked.

"These findings challenge longstanding assumptions that certain biomolecules such as hemoglobin cannot survive deep time," Professor Grice said.

"It opens exciting new avenues for molecular-level paleontology, allowing us to investigate the evolution of blood, metabolism and even activity levels in ancient animals."

Such information could eventually help researchers better understand how extinct animals functioned, including aspects of their metabolism and physiology that are difficult to reconstruct from bones alone.

Implications for Ancient Life Beyond Earth

The significance of the discovery may extend well beyond dinosaurs. Understanding how fragile biological structures can survive for millions of years could also help scientists identify possible traces of ancient life in other extreme environments, including those beyond Earth.

Professor Martin Van Kranendonk, head of Curtin University's School of Earth and Planetary Sciences, said the results are changing how researchers understand the preservation of molecular structures over vast timescales and under harsh conditions.

These insights could be valuable to astrobiology, a field that investigates the possibility of life elsewhere in the universe. If biological molecules or their chemical signatures can persist under the right conditions for more than 100 million years, scientists may need to reconsider where and how they look for evidence of ancient organisms.

"This study exemplifies how coordinated efforts across institutions, continents and scientific disciplines can unlock extraordinary insights into ancient life," Professor Van Kranendonk said.

The research was supported by a 2021 Australian Research Council Laureate Fellowship awarded to Professor Grice.

The study, titled "Heme signatures in mineralized red blood cells within vascular canals of a 115- million-year-old dinosaur bone," was published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

Using the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), astronomers have discovered the oldest pair of supermassive black hole-powered quasars ever seen. There's just one problem: they shouldn't exist!

The compact quasar pair, spotted with the aid of the Gemini North telescope, has been designated J1602+4228AB and nicknamed Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua, which means "Two celestial bodies of fathomless powerful darkness in the brilliance of heat reincarnating energy into the universe." The compact quasar pair is seen as it was 900 million years after the Big Bang at a time when such supermassive black holes should not have had time to grow to such tremendous masses.

Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua isn't just the oldest and most distant quasar pairing ever seen. There is just 18,100 light-years, or roughly one-fifth the diameter of the Milky Way, between the supermassive black holes, which have masses of 1.5 billion and 400 million times that of the sun. That makes Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua the most compact quasar pair found during a period of the universe's history known as Cosmic Dawn, shortly after the birth of the first stars, galaxies, and black holes.

"There is no definitive theoretical explanation for how a single one of these giant quasars exists so early in the age of our universe, much less two," research team leader Silvia Onorato of the NOIRLab said in a statement.

"We observed Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua at a time when the universe was only a thirteenth of its age and, astonishingly, its supermassive black holes are just as massive as those we see today."

Quasars occur when the supermassive black holes that sit at the heart of large galaxies are surrounded by a flattened cloud of swirling gas and dust called an "accretion disk," from which they feed or "accrete" matter. The immense gravity of the central black hole causes friction, heating the accretion disk and causing it to glow, often brighter than the combined light of every star in the surrounding galaxy. We see that glow as a quasar.

Finding such objects in the recent cosmic history of the 13.8-billion-year-old universe isn't troubling, though finding compact pairs of them is still extremely rare. Such pairs should be common because the merger of galaxies that brings together supermassive black holes is frequent. That should lead to an abundance of pairs of quasars with a separation less than the typical size of a galaxy. There are three reasons this has proven tricky. Firstly, the "quasar phase" of a supermassive black hole is relatively short on cosmic terms. Secondly, even relatively close quasar pairs are very far away, making them faint and hard to detect with ground-based telescopes. Finally, at such great distances and with such a small separation between the two supermassive black holes, the individual members of a quasar pair are hard to individually resolve.

Yet, astronomers do find quasar pairs. Sometimes at distances and times that they would probably rather not, because it challenges everything we know about black hole growth.

The trouble arises before the universe was 1 billion years. That is because, according to current models, black holes should need at least 1 billion years to feed and merge enough to reach masses millions or billions of times that of the sun.

Yet, since it began operations in 2022, the JWST has been routinely discovering supermassive black holes powering quasars as early as 400 million years after the Big Bang. If that wasn't confusing enough, the discovery of Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua, the third quasar pair seen at Cosmic Dawn, could really break current models.

Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua was uncovered in data from the JWST's Aether survey, which is conducting a census of objects in the early universe. Using JWST’s NIRSpec (Near-Infrared Spectrograph Integral Field Unit) instrument, the survey has uncovered 200 quasars, just under half of all currently known early universe quasars. It was while browsing the Aether dataset that the team discovered that quasar J1602+4228A is not alone, it had a companion now designated J1602+4228B.

Resolving these two quasars should have been nearly impossible from the ground. But this was possible for Gemini North thanks to perfect timing and perfect weather conditions over Maunakea, the dormant volcano on the island of Hawai'i where the telescope is located.

A definite scientific feat, Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua remains a mystery for now, but it could actually help scientists better understand how galaxies were coming together during Cosmic Dawn, a vital stage in the evolution of the universe.

"Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua is a really unique environment," Onorato said. "It's a laboratory for astronomers to study how the very first massive galaxies and their central black holes assembled together through direct galaxy interactions during these early times."

The team's results were published on Tuesday (Nov. 10) The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

#735. NASA’s Swift telescope falls to Earth after nearly 22 years in space

NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory has returned to Earth after spending nearly 22 years in space, bringing an extraordinary era of astronomical discovery to a close. The spacecraft re-entered Earth's atmosphere on Wednesday, ending a mission that lasted more than ten times longer than originally planned.

Launched in 2004, Swift was a pioneering space observatory equipped with three telescopes designed to study some of the most powerful explosions in the universe. Its instruments could detect different types of light, allowing scientists to investigate energetic cosmic events that would be difficult to understand using a single telescope.

NASA's Swift Observatory Re-Enters Earth's Atmosphere

The U.S. Space Force confirmed that Swift entered the atmosphere at 7:39 a.m. EST on Wednesday above North Sumatra, Indonesia. The reported location was approximately 3.4 degrees north latitude and 98.6 degrees east longitude.

NASA anticipated that most of the spacecraft would burn up as it plunged through the atmosphere. However, officials acknowledged that some components might have survived the intense heat of re-entry.

A Two-Year NASA Mission That Lasted Nearly 22 Years

Swift was originally developed to investigate gamma-ray bursts, extraordinarily powerful flashes of high-energy radiation associated with some of the most extreme events in the cosmos. These bursts can occur when massive stars collapse or when certain compact objects, such as neutron stars, merge.

Although NASA initially planned for Swift to operate for just two years, the observatory continued making scientific contributions for more than two decades.

One of its most important capabilities was its ability to respond quickly to sudden cosmic events. When Swift detected an energetic outburst, it could rapidly redirect its telescopes toward the source and notify observatories around the world. This coordinated approach allowed astronomers to study brief astronomical phenomena before they faded from view.

Swift also observed multiple wavelengths of light, giving researchers different ways to examine the same event and better understand the physical processes behind it.

Over its remarkably long lifetime, Swift's scientific contributions expanded far beyond its original focus on gamma-ray bursts.

The observatory helped astronomers investigate active galaxies powered by supermassive black holes, stars that produce powerful X-ray flares, and supernovae, the enormous explosions that mark the deaths of certain stars.

Its observations also extended much closer to home, including studies of comets and asteroids within our own solar system.

By combining rapid observations with the ability to detect different forms of radiation, Swift became a valuable tool for exploring both distant cosmic explosions and nearby objects. Its re-entry marks the end of a mission that greatly exceeded its planned lifespan and helped transform scientists' understanding of some of the universe's most energetic phenomena.

Ancient Roman cities, temples and amphitheaters across the Mediterranean will fall into the moon's shadow during the total solar eclipse on Aug. 2, 2027.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Ancient Egyptian temples will inevitably dominate the story of the total solar eclipse on Aug. 2, 2027.

After all, the path of totality crosses Luxor, home to Karnak, the Valley of the Kings, and some of the ancient world's most famous monuments. But follow the moon's shadow west and another ancient civilization comes into view. Before reaching Egypt, totality will sweep across the Mediterranean and North Africa, passing over an extraordinary collection of Roman cities, fortresses, theaters, temples and triumphal arches. Many lie within what became Rome's North African provinces, a region that produced some of the empire's wealthiest and most impressive cities.

From beachside Baelo Claudia in Spain and military Tamuda in Morocco to Timgad and Djémila in Algeria and the jaw-dropping El Jem Amphitheater in Tunisia, Roman ruins will experience between two and more than five minutes of darkness — creating extraordinary possibilities for eclipse chasers and photographers. Here are some of the best places to watch the moon's shadow cross what was once the Roman Empire. All times, totality durations and historical cloud cover data come from Time and Date.

Start of totality and duration: 10:44 a.m. CEST; 4 minutes, 31 seconds

Altitude of the sun: 37 degrees above east

Roman ruins, an Atlantic beach and the mountains of Africa could all share the frame with the eclipsed sun at Baelo Claudia. Founded in the second century B.C., this remarkably well-preserved Roman city near Bolonia beach includes a forum, basilica, theater, temples, baths and a decumanus maximus (east-west street), all set against forested hills and a vast coastal sand dune. For photographers, the possibilities are exceptional — columns and temples may provide an ancient foreground, while wider compositions could incorporate the beach and dunes. On particularly clear days, Morocco is visible across the Strait of Gibraltar — potentially putting Roman ruins, two continents and a total solar eclipse into one extraordinary scene.

Start of totality and duration: 10:48 a.m. CEST; 1 minute, 57 seconds

Altitude of the sun: 39 degrees above east

Few eclipse locations can offer two civilizations in the same photograph. Málaga's Roman Theatre was built in the first century B.C., when the city was part of the Roman province of Hispania, and today sits directly beneath the Alcazaba, the imposing Muslim-era palace-fortress that dominates the hillside above. Although its totality is considerably shorter than locations farther south, the photographic possibilities are compelling. From a carefully chosen position, it may be possible to frame the darkened sun with the theater's ancient stonework and the walls of the Alcazaba rising behind it. Another major advantage for eclipse chasers is that this extraordinary historical setting sits in the heart of Málaga, making it one of the most accessible ancient sites on the path of totality.

Start of totality and duration: 08:45 a.m. GMT; 4 minutes, 51 seconds

Altitude of sun: 38 degrees above east-southeast

Long before the Romans arrived in northern Morocco, Tamuda was already a thriving Mauretanian settlement. Founded around the third century B.C. in the Martil Valley, near modern Tétouan, the Romans established a fortified military camp here in the first century A.D., whose massive stone walls remain the defining feature of this archaeological site. Tamuda combines long totality, promising weather and an atmospheric archaeological foreground — yet remains far less famous than the Roman sites across the Strait of Gibraltar.

Start of totality and duration: 10:01 a.m. CET; 5 minutes, 20 seconds

Altitude of sun: 51 degrees above east-southeast

Few places in the 2027 path of totality combine ancient architecture and long totality quite like Timgad. Founded around A.D. 100 as the Roman colony of Thamugadi, this remarkably well-preserved city sits on an open plateau at the foot of Algeria's Aurès Mountains. Its grid of streets, forum, theater, temples, baths and columns survives alongside its most famous monument, the three-arched gateway traditionally known as the Arch of Trajan. A relatively high sun will make close architectural compositions challenging, but Timgad's wide-open site provides plenty of possibilities for carefully planned wide-angle images.

Start of totality and duration: 10:01 a.m. CET; 5 minutes, 20 seconds

Altitude of sun: 51 degrees above east-southeast

Just 12—15 miles (20—25 km) west of Timgad lies its military counterpart. Lambaesis was the principal base of Rome's Legio III Augusta, the legion that helped secure Rome's African Empire. Rather than an entire gridded colonial city, the attraction here is monumental military architecture, most notably the imposing remains of the heart of the fortress. The eclipse circumstances are almost identical to nearby Timgad, with more than five minutes of totality and historically excellent prospects for clear skies. Scout both sites beforehand, study where the sun will stand above the ruins, and decide which offers the strongest alignment — and the easiest access — on eclipse morning.

Start of totality and duration: 10:02 a.m. CET; 2 minutes, 2 seconds

Altitude of eclipsed sun: 50 degrees above east-southeast

Djémila trades a long eclipse for one of the most spectacular settings on the path of totality. Known to the Romans as Cuicul, this exceptionally well-preserved city was built in mountainous terrain around 2,950 feet (900 meters) above sea level — an unusual setting for a Roman settlement — and its ruins include temples, forums, houses, baths, arches and a theater. The surrounding green hills and mountains give eclipse photographers a very different backdrop from the flatter, more arid landscapes farther south. The catch is totality, which is significantly shorter than at other Roman ruins.

Start of totality and duration: 10:06 a.m. CET; 5 minutes, 19 seconds

Altitude of sun: 54 degrees above east-southeast

Sbeitla could be one of the great archaeological settings for the 2027 eclipse. Known in Roman times as Sufetula, the city prospered under Roman rule and today contains some of Tunisia's most impressive ancient ruins. Its centerpiece is an unusual group of three remarkably well-preserved temples dedicated to Jupiter, Juno and Minerva, standing above the forum and reached through the monumental Arch of Antoninus Pius. That high sun will require some careful positioning and probably a wide-angle composition, but eclipse photographers will have an extraordinary collection of arches, columns and temples to use as foregrounds.

Start of totality and duration: 10:09 a.m. CET; 4 minutes, 23 seconds

Altitude of eclipsed sun: 56 degrees above east-southeast

It may be the third-largest and one of the best-preserved Roman amphitheaters in the world, but El Jem offers another reason to consider it for totality. Unlike Rome's Colosseum — which it closely resembles — visitors can explore its multi-tiered seating, climb high into the surviving structure for panoramic views and visit the underground passages once used by gladiators and animals. Built around A.D. 238, El Jem combines one of Rome's greatest surviving monuments with some of the most promising eclipse conditions on the entire track.

The Vespera III is a premium smart telescope that delivers powerful features like multi-night observation and mosaic technology, rewarding avid astrophotographers who have a serious interest in capturing the night sky.

Excellent deep-sky images with rich colors

Multi-night imaging makes ambitious targets easier

Much more expensive than many of its rivals

Why you can trust Space.com Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test and review products.

I’ve spent a lot of time with smart telescopes, from relatively inexpensive Seestar models to the original Vaonis Vespera and the Vespera Pro. They all promise essentially the same thing — you put a telescope outside at night, choose something interesting on your smartphone and let the technology take care of the rest. The Vaonis Vespera 3 does that exceptionally well, but after spending several nights with it, I’m convinced it’s designed for a rather different kind of buyer.

At $2,490/£2,199, this is hardly an impulse purchase for the beginner who’s curious about astronomy – you could buy several perfectly capable smart telescopes for the same money. Yet I found myself increasingly impressed by what the Vespera 3 could achieve, particularly when I returned to the same object over several nights. The images were sharp, the colors were excellent and I almost never had to think about the battery.

That doesn’t mean the experience was flawless. I sometimes spent longer than I’d have liked waiting for the telescope to get ready, but once it began photographing the sky, the Vespera 3 reminded me why I love smart telescopes so much.

One of my favorite things about smart telescopes is watching a photograph develop as more light is collected. What begins as a fairly ordinary patch of stars gradually becomes something much more interesting. First a faint cloud of gas appears, then more structure emerges, and eventually you have an image that, only a few short years ago, would have been difficult to capture without specialist equipment.

With the Vespera 3, I spent several nights photographing the Pleiades (M45), the famous star cluster in Taurus. The Pleiades make an excellent subject for testing a telescope because the stars are bright, but the surrounding nebulosity is much harder to capture convincingly. The Singularity app used to control Vespera 3 stacks each image as it goes, but keeps them in sight as an optional time-lapse, so you can see exactly why you’re spending so much time on one object.

Even better, the Vespera 3’s PerseverENS feature lets you add data to an existing observation over multiple nights (it’s actually called multi-night observation in the app). Instead of having to call it a night or start again every time the weather interrupts an imaging session, you can return to a target and continue building the image over weeks — or years. This is excellent for faint nebulas, but also for anyone who lives somewhere with unpredictable weather.

The Vespera 3 also has CovalENS, Vaonis’s mosaic imaging system, which captures adjacent sections of sky to produce a larger image. That’s helpful for objects such as the Pleiades and large nebulas, which occupy a substantial area of the sky.

Mosaics inevitably take longer than conventional images — if it images six sections of the night sky, it takes six times longer for the same image quality — but they also make the telescope more versatile than its native field of view (2.5 x 1.4 degrees) might suggest.

Smart telescopes are particularly useful for people living under light-polluted skies. A conventional optical telescope can show you the moon, the planets and some brighter star clusters, but faint nebulas are largely out of reach. The Vespera 3 tackles that problem by taking repeated short exposures and combining them automatically. As the exposures accumulate, faint details become clearer, and the image becomes less noisy.

I photographed the Orion Nebula (M42), one of the most rewarding deep-sky targets for almost any telescope. Its bright central region makes it a quick capture, but the surrounding clouds of gas give a camera plenty more to uncover. The color in M42 via the Vespera 3 was particularly striking: stars looked sharp, the background was pleasingly clean, but the colors had a richness you don’t always see from less expensive models.

The Vespera 3 uses a 50mm refractor telescope and an 8.3-megapixel Sony IMX585 camera sensor. Those specifications are identical to the Vespera 2, but the Vespera 3 has a new optical system, which uses four lenses in three groups, including two extra-low-dispersion elements. Vaonis has also introduced internal baffling to reduce unwanted reflections from nearby artificial lights. For urban astronomers, every little helps. I wouldn’t claim that the Vespera 3 makes dark skies unnecessary. It doesn’t — and if you do take a trip to dark skies with the Vespera 3, your images will improve — but it can produce extremely satisfying images even from a city.

For anyone who wants more control over their images, the Vespera 3 also saves lossless TIFF files that can be exported to a PC or Mac using a USB-C cable. That means you can take the images into your preferred editing software for further processing, rather than relying entirely on the results produced by the Singularity app.

There’s something wonderfully simple about looking at a map of the night sky, spotting an interesting object and tapping it to point your scope in that direction. It’s one of the reasons I enjoy using Seestar smart telescopes. I did miss that experience with the Vespera 3.

Vaonis’s Singularity app has an extensive catalog of galaxies, nebulas, star clusters and other targets, but I found myself browsing lists when I’d rather have been exploring an interactive sky chart.

There is a section devoted to constellations, which initially got my hopes up. I thought it might allow me to photograph an entire constellation, capturing its familiar star pattern as a wide-field image. Sadly not — each constellation has a diagram showing where the catalog’s deep-sky objects are located. That’s useful if you already know what you’re looking for, but it isn’t the same as being able to see the sky overhead and choose a target visually.

However, the telescope can still find and photograph the objects in its catalog, and the automated tracking works well once you’ve made your choice.

That smart telescopes give you instant gratification is something of a selling point — but it’s also a myth. Yes, they save an enormous amount of work compared with traditional astrophotography equipment. There’s no separate tracking mount to align, no camera to attach and no laptop required to control the imaging process. However, automation doesn’t necessarily mean instant results.

For example, every time the Vespera 3 is switched on, it needs to establish its position by identifying stars overhead. Its Star Zone Search and autofocus procedure took around five minutes, with a percentage displayed in the app to show how far it had progressed. That’s not an unreasonable wait for a sophisticated astronomical instrument, but it felt a little drawn-out when I was eager to begin photographing something. If there are clouds, expect it to take much longer.

Once the Vespera 3 had aligned itself, I could choose a target and leave the telescope to work. The optical arm moved into position, the camera began collecting exposures and an image gradually appeared on my smartphone.

I was less impressed by the touch-sensitive power button. Its softly illuminated indicator didn’t always make it obvious whether the telescope was switched on. More than once, I had to check my phone’s available Wi-Fi networks to establish whether it was on or off.

Vaonis claims the Vespera 3 can operate for up to 11 hours. I didn’t run it continuously until the battery was exhausted, but it lasted longer than every observing session I attempted. That did change how I used it, because I could concentrate on the target instead of keeping an eye on the remaining charge or wondering whether I should connect a portable battery.

The new, improved tripod also makes a difference. It’s tall, adjustable and reassuringly stable, with a useful canopy strung between its legs for holding any accessories — perhaps filters, a red torch or snacks.

The Vespera 3 is capable of photographing the moon and the sun, although solar photography requires a properly fitted optional solar filter. Unfortunately, that costs a further $179/£159, which is rather steep.

It’s also not the best choice for detailed planetary images. The 245mm focal length is ideal for framing many galaxies and nebulas, but Jupiter and Saturn remain small subjects.

Another omission is an equatorial tracking mode. Some cheaper smart telescopes — such as the Seestar S50 Pro and the DwarfLab Dwarf 3 — offer EQ mode for more advanced imaging, but the Vespera 3 relies solely on its motorized alt-azimuth mount. That doesn’t stop it from producing excellent photographs, but it does mean more experienced users have one less option to experiment with.

The biggest question surrounding the Vespera 3 isn’t whether it works — it’s whether it’s worth the money. After all, it costs far more than the Seestar S50 Pro, which also has built-in imaging filters, whereas the Vespera’s light pollution ($229/£219), dual-band ($399/£370) and solar (£179/£159) filters are optional purchases. They do, however, make a significant difference — with the dual-band filter giving nebulas more contrast, color and detail.

Overall, the Vespera 3 offers a slightly more polished imaging experience than the many entry-level smart telescopes on the market. I enjoyed its clean, colorful images and appreciated the ability to work on the same subject over several nights, while the excellent tripod and battery endurance make it particularly well suited to longer observing sessions.

I wouldn’t recommend it to everyone, but I can see why someone who already loves photographing the night sky might happily pay extra for the Vespera 3.
