#663. Alzheimer’s may have early warning signs outside the brain

Alzheimer's disease is best known for its effects on memory and thinking, but new research suggests that some symptoms may develop in a surprising place: outside the brain.

Scientists at the University of Central Florida (UCF) have discovered that genetic mutations associated with Alzheimer's can interfere with the nerves that control muscle movement, even without involvement from the brain or spinal cord. The findings could help explain why some people with Alzheimer's experience changes in walking, balance, or coordination long before noticeable memory problems emerge.

The discovery raises the possibility that movement difficulties could provide earlier warning signs of the disease and that treatments focused exclusively on the brain may overlook important problems elsewhere in the body.

The research was led by James Hickman, a professor at UCF's Nanoscience Technology Center, and Research Professor Xiufang "Nadine" Guo, working alongside scientists at the healthcare technology company Hesperos. Funded by the National Institutes of Health's National Institute on Aging, the study used laboratory systems built from human cells to investigate how inherited Alzheimer's mutations affect movement. The findings were published in Alzheimer's & Dementia: The Journal of the Alzheimer's Association.

"Motor deficits may be an earlier indication [of Alzheimer's]," Guo says. "If we can detect those changes and intervene earlier, that could help delay the onset of central nervous system symptoms."

Why Alzheimer's Symptoms May Appear Before Memory Loss

Alzheimer's is generally associated with progressive memory loss, confusion, and declining cognitive abilities. However, doctors have also observed that some patients develop physical symptoms, including changes in balance, coordination, and gait (manner of walking), years before clear cognitive difficulties become apparent.

These observations have raised an important question: Are such movement problems simply a consequence of damage occurring in the brain, or could Alzheimer's also interfere directly with nerves elsewhere in the body?

To investigate, the UCF team focused on familial Alzheimer's, a rare inherited form of the disease that typically develops earlier in life (from 40 to 65 years of age) than the more common form.

Their experiments revealed that motor neurons carrying mutations linked to familial Alzheimer's could disrupt the connections responsible for controlling muscles, even when the brain and spinal cord were completely absent from the experimental system.

Motor neurons are specialized nerve cells that transmit signals to muscles, telling them when to contract and produce movement. The new findings suggest that Alzheimer's mutations can interfere with this process directly, rather than affecting movement only through damage to the brain.

"This is the first time it's been demonstrated that deficits in the peripheral nervous system can arise directly from these mutations," Hickman says. "It means drugs that target the brain may not fix problems in the rest of the body."

The peripheral nervous system includes the nerves located outside the brain and spinal cord. These nerves carry signals between the central nervous system and the rest of the body, helping control movement, sensation, and other essential functions.

Guo also points out that preserving the ability to move could have benefits beyond physical health. Regular physical activity is associated with better cognitive well-being, so protecting motor function may also help support brain health.

How a Miniature Human Cell System Revealed the Discovery

To examine the relationship between Alzheimer's mutations and muscle movement, the scientists used an innovative laboratory platform known as "human-on-a-chip" technology.

Developed and manufactured through Hesperos, a company co-founded by Hickman, these miniature systems bring different types of human cells together under controlled conditions. They allow researchers to recreate specific biological functions and observe how diseases interfere with them.

Unlike conventional laboratory experiments that examine isolated cells, these systems can reproduce important interactions between different tissues. They also provide an alternative to animal models, which do not always accurately reflect how human diseases behave.

For this study, the team created a miniature model of the neuromuscular junction, the connection where a motor neuron communicates with a muscle cell.

The model was deliberately designed without a brain or spinal cord. This was a crucial part of the experiment because it allowed the researchers to investigate whether Alzheimer's-related changes could cause movement problems independently of the central nervous system.

The scientists combined healthy muscle cells with motor neurons derived from stem cells that carried genetic mutations associated with familial Alzheimer's disease. Stem cells are cells that can develop into specialized types of cells, making them valuable tools for studying human diseases in the laboratory.

The researchers then examined how effectively the altered nerve cells communicated with otherwise healthy muscle tissue.

The results showed that the Alzheimer's-associated mutations could interfere with normal nerve-to-muscle function. This suggests that at least some movement difficulties linked to the disease may arise directly in the peripheral nervous system rather than being caused entirely by degeneration in the brain.

Why Damaged Nerve Connections Can Affect Walking and Balance

Every voluntary movement depends on successful communication between the nervous system and the muscles.

At the neuromuscular junction, an electrical signal traveling along a motor neuron triggers chemical communication that causes a muscle to contract. This process makes everyday activities possible, from walking and maintaining posture to lifting objects and performing precise movements.

When the connection becomes impaired, muscles may respond less effectively to nerve signals. Depending on the severity and location of the problem, this can contribute to weakness, reduced coordination, and difficulty sustaining physical activity.

To evaluate these effects, the research team measured how consistently nerve signals produced muscle contractions and how long the muscles could continue contracting before becoming fatigued.

These measurements provided a direct assessment of how well the nerve and muscle cells worked together. They also resemble aspects of the functional testing physicians use when examining patients with movement disorders.

"You can't move unless the motor circuit works," Hickman says. "When a doctor taps your knee to check your reflex, they're testing that exact connection."

By demonstrating impaired nerve-to-muscle communication in a system containing no brain or spinal cord, the study provides evidence that mutations linked to familial Alzheimer's can produce effects beyond the central nervous system.

However, the experiments do not establish that these changes necessarily occur before memory loss in patients. Further research will be needed to determine how closely the laboratory findings reflect the progression of Alzheimer's in people, particularly those with the more common forms of the disease.

Could This Discovery Lead to Earlier Alzheimer's Detection?

The findings suggest a potentially important new direction for Alzheimer's research: looking beyond memory and other cognitive symptoms when investigating the disease.

If future studies confirm that changes in motor function are detectable early in certain patients, tests of walking, coordination, or nerve-to-muscle activity might eventually help identify disease-related changes before more obvious neurological symptoms develop.

The results also raise questions about treatment. Many Alzheimer's therapies are designed to address processes occurring in the brain, but medications that target the central nervous system may not necessarily correct abnormalities affecting peripheral nerves and muscles.

Understanding these separate effects could help researchers investigate treatments that protect physical function alongside cognitive health.

Human-on-a-Chip Technology Could Transform Disease Research

Beyond the implications for Alzheimer's, the researchers see considerable potential in using human-on-a-chip systems to investigate other diseases and evaluate possible treatments.

Because these platforms contain human cells and reproduce measurable biological activities, they can help scientists observe disease-related changes in conditions that more closely resemble human physiology than some conventional experimental models.

This approach may be particularly useful in drug development, where researchers need to understand not only how a potential treatment affects individual cells but also how it influences interactions between different tissues.

Such systems can also uncover biological effects that may be difficult to detect in animal experiments, potentially helping researchers identify promising therapies and recognize limitations earlier in development.

For Hickman, the progress represents the culmination of three decades of work devoted to understanding disease through more realistic laboratory models.

"These systems let us study disease in a way that's closer to what actually happens in the human body, and that's what we need to develop better treatments," he says.

"It’s amazing that by using radio wavelengths, we can detect the storms on a star over 5,000 light-years away."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Astronomers have traced a mysterious radio signal back to a cosmic odd couple comprised of a dead star, a white dwarf, and its stellar companion, a sun-like star.

The white dwarf in the newly discovered system, designated GPM J071507−114153 and located around 5,000 light-years away, spins once every eight minutes, sending out radio pulses. These radio pulses have been seen from binary systems with smaller and cooler red dwarf stars before, but rarely from a system like GPM J071507−114153.

GPM J071507−114153 belongs to a class of celestial objects called long-period transients (LPTs) known to produce radio signals that switch on and off over intervals of minutes or hours. Around a dozen LPTs have been detected since the team behind this research found the first in 2021. Several previously discovered LPT systems contain a white dwarf and a companion star, but it has been unclear which of the two stars was generating the radio pulses. That means the discovery of GPM J071507−114153 and finding that the pulses come from close to the white dwarf could be a significant step toward understanding the nature of LPTs.

"This is the first time the pulses are clear enough to see the white dwarf moving in its orbit around its companion," team leader and commissioning scientist with the Square Kilometre Array Observatory (SKA), Sam McSweeney, said in a statement. "So we know that the pulsations are coming from a region close to the white dwarf, or possibly even from the white dwarf itself."

The pulses seen by the team also allowed them to detect stellar flares erupting on the sun-like star.

"As a bonus, we also saw the white dwarf moving behind a region with a strong magnetic field, most likely a 'stellar prominence,' which is a large loop of plasma erupting from a star's surface," team member Natasha Hurley-Walker of the International Centre for Radio Astronomy Research (ICRAR), Curtin University, Australia, said. "It's amazing that by using radio wavelengths we can detect the storms on a star over 5,000 light-years away."

Hurley-Walker and the team at ICRAR have been at the cutting edge of rare star systems like this.

"We detected this system in a large survey using the Murchison Widefield Array (MWA) to scan the entire Milky Way visible from Australia," Hurley-Walker said. "We then used the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa to determine its precise position."

After the radio telescopes detected this LPT, it was confirmed using the W.M. Keck Observatory on Maunakea in Hawaii. The visible light follow-up of Keck also confirmed that the star in GPM J071507−114153 was a G-type star, just like the sun.

MeerKAT and the MWA are both precursors for the Square Kilometre Array (SKA), the world’s largest and most sensitive radio telescope project. That means the future is bright for LPTs.

"If we are already making such discoveries with precursor telescopes, just imagine how many more star systems we will be able to find, and what a beautifully detailed view of their signals we will have, once the SKA telescopes are completely built," McSweeney said.

The team's research was published on Thursday (Nov. 12) in the journal Nature Astronomy.

Robert Lea is a science journalist in the U.K. whose articles have been published in Physics World, New Scientist, Astronomy Magazine, All About Space, Newsweek and ZME Science. #659. Scientists uncover a 192-year-old mystery hidden in a mangled silver coin

A badly distorted British silver coin dating to 1834 may hold evidence of an unusual accident during the minting process nearly 200 years ago. New scientific analysis suggests that the remarkable damage to the coin was more likely caused by a manufacturing problem than by ordinary wear, corrosion, or a later impact.

The findings, reported by IA STUDIO in the journal npj Heritage Science, center on a silver sixpence issued during the reign of King William IV. The coin was found in an album containing various coins at a car boot sale in Greater Manchester, England. Although the sixpence had an individual price tag of £8, the entire album was subsequently purchased as a single lot rather than the coin being bought separately.

What makes this particular sixpence remarkable is the extent and unusual pattern of its damage. Its central surface appears severely crushed and distorted, yet much of the outer rim and the small grooves along its edge remain relatively intact. The contrast raised an intriguing question about what could have happened to the coin.

To investigate, researchers examined the silver piece using powerful microscopes, chemical testing, and detailed three-dimensional surface measurements. The results point toward an unusual sequence of intense compression, potentially while the coin was being struck at the mint.

A Crushed Silver Coin Reveals Unusual Clues

The most striking evidence came from the coin's severely distorted central regions. Detailed measurements revealed deep, sharply defined depressions, elevated ridges, stepped surfaces, and areas where the metal appeared to have been pushed and displaced in overlapping patterns.

These features were particularly pronounced on the front of the coin, known as the obverse, which bears the portrait of William IV. Across the damaged central portrait area, the difference between the highest and lowest measured points reached approximately 0.75 millimeters.

That may sound small, but it represents a substantial distortion on the surface of a thin silver coin.

The investigators found that the overall damage was most consistent with repeated applications of high pressure concentrated in a limited area. The metal also appears to have been at least partly prevented from spreading outward as the force was applied.

This combination of heavy central damage and relatively well-preserved edges is difficult to reconcile with the gradual effects of circulation or simple corrosion. It also makes a single later impact, with the metal free to move outward, a less convincing explanation.

Instead, the findings favor an unusual problem during the original striking process, although the available evidence does not establish the exact sequence of events with certainty.

Microscopic Analysis Reveals Damage Beneath the Surface

To better understand the unusual deformation, the investigation combined scanning electron microscopy with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (SEM-EDX) and optical surface profilometry.

The microscopic and chemical examinations provided information about the coin's metal composition and the changes affecting its surface.

In areas that had escaped the worst damage, testing identified an underlying silver and copper alloy. The more severely distorted regions contained lower measured concentrations of silver, higher levels of copper, and additional chemical evidence associated with corrosion and contamination.

These substances were especially concentrated inside the depressions formed by the damaged metal.

However, the chemical results largely reflected changes at the surface. Although corrosion and contamination had affected the coin, they could not adequately account for the depth, shape, and distribution of its unusual distortions.

The team also used optical surface profilometry, a technique that maps the height and shape of a surface in three dimensions. This made it possible to examine the coin's damaged areas in much greater detail than ordinary photographs could provide.

The resulting maps showed steep depressions, raised shoulders, abrupt changes in surface height, and multiple layers of metal displacement.

Using height measurements supplied by the Oxford Materials Characterisation Service, the study's author determined that the damaged central portrait region varied in height by approximately 750 micrometers, equivalent to 0.75 millimeters.

Taken together, the findings suggest that the coin underwent repeated compression while its sideways movement was at least partly restricted. This explanation fits the evidence better than ordinary wear, which generally smooths a coin's surface over time, or corrosion, which tends to remove or chemically alter material.

A Rare Glimpse Into 19th-Century Coin Production

The sixpence was produced in 1834, when Britain was already using steam-powered presses to manufacture coins.

During this period, coins with serious striking defects were typically identified through mint inspections and melted down so the metal could be reused. This was especially important for coins made from precious metals such as silver.

If the unusual deformation occurred during the original minting process, the sixpence may therefore represent a rare surviving example of a manufacturing failure that would ordinarily have been removed from circulation before it ever reached the public.

Such a coin could provide a physical record of a brief mechanical problem during the early era of mechanized coin production.

Determining whether the damage actually occurred at the mint is challenging, however. Historic metal objects can undergo many changes over decades or centuries, and severe deformation may obscure the physical clues needed to identify its origin.

To address this uncertainty, the study examined several kinds of evidence independently. The researchers considered the composition of the underlying metal, chemical changes at the surface, and the three-dimensional geometry of the deformation before comparing the results with different possible explanations.

The findings also demonstrate how non-destructive scientific techniques can be used to investigate other historic metal objects. By combining chemical and structural evidence, researchers may be able to distinguish manufacturing defects from later damage even when visual inspection alone provides no clear answer.

How AI Helped Investigate the Coin Mystery

The investigation also explored how computational tools, including artificial intelligence, could assist in evaluating a historical mystery without replacing physical scientific evidence.

Before any laboratory results were available, the author began by studying high-resolution photographs of the sixpence and systematically reviewing its unusual surface features.

This early examination helped identify several possible causes of the damage and establish what kinds of physical measurements would be needed to test them.

Human-supervised computational tools, including large language models (LLMs), helped organize the observations, develop alternative explanations, compare competing ideas, and formulate questions that could later be investigated through laboratory testing.

Importantly, the initial hypotheses and analytical notes were recorded before the independently produced laboratory measurements became available.

The possible explanations included ordinary circulation wear and corrosion, mechanical damage occurring after minting, later compression under restricted conditions, and deformation during the original manufacturing process.

To investigate these possibilities, independent measurements were commissioned from the Experimental Techniques Centre at Brunel University of London and the Oxford Materials Characterisation Service within the Department of Materials at the University of Oxford.

Once the testing was completed, computational tools were used again to help organize the resulting data and compare the physical findings with the earlier explanations.

"The important sequence was hypothesis first, independent laboratory measurement second," said A. Ikraam, founder of IA STUDIO and author of the study.

"We used the models to ask what features mattered and what evidence could distinguish one explanation from another. Then the laboratory measurements gave us something physical to test those ideas against. The models could support the reasoning process, but they could not decide what happened to the coin."

Scientific Evidence Points to a Possible Minting Error

Although artificial intelligence played a supporting role in organizing observations and evaluating competing possibilities, it did not produce the laboratory measurements or determine the final findings.

The study's conclusions were based on independently generated scientific data, with the author retaining responsibility for interpreting the evidence and deciding which explanation was best supported.

The results favor a rare minting anomaly involving repeated, highly concentrated pressure, rather than damage caused by ordinary circulation, corrosion, or a single unrestricted impact after production. Nevertheless, the research does not conclusively establish every detail of what happened to the sixpence.

Beyond shedding light on the possible origins of a strangely mangled 1834 coin, the investigation illustrates how modern imaging, chemical analysis, and carefully evaluated computational tools can work together to uncover clues hidden in historic objects.

What initially appeared to be little more than a badly damaged silver coin may instead preserve an unusual record of how something went wrong during the early days of mechanized coin manufacturing.

#657. The Polar Vortex Is About to Make Weather Weird From the UK to the US

A critical blockade against some of nature’s coldest air has temporarily broken down—and much earlier in the year than normal. Disruptions in this circulation, known as the polar vortex, often push intensely cold air out of the Arctic toward lower latitudes.

Experts still aren’t entirely sure how the current collapse will play out in our everyday weather. But it’s another sign that we may be in for a wild ride over the weeks and months to come.

The polar vortex is a band of upper-level winds wrapping around the Arctic Circle like a dam. This circulation is usually strong and stable, helping to keep the season’s coldest air locked near the North Pole. But the winds occasionally weaken or even reverse course, which can set off an atmospheric chain reaction, allowing bitterly cold air to spill southward.

The manner in which the polar vortex breaks down determines what kind of weather conditions we might expect. Upper-level winds dipping southward in troughs are responsible for brief spells of cold temperatures. These “lobes” of the polar vortex, as they’re known, are relatively common in a typical winter.

Sometimes, this circulation can splinter into smaller pieces. If the vortex were a flowing river, these fragments are like leaves stuck on the riverbank, forcing extremely cold air to linger over the same areas for days or weeks at a time.

One such case made this phenomenon a household name. A highly disrupted polar vortex in early 2015 sent a weeks-long burst of cold air sweeping over the eastern US. Chicago recorded its coldest February in nearly 140 years. In Lexington, Kentucky, temperatures bottomed out at –18 degrees Fahrenheit, as subfreezing air dove all the way to the Gulf of Mexico.

Seeing a breakdown of the polar vortex this early in the season is unprecedented in the historical record. Disruptions of this extent typically don’t occur until the latter half of winter. Based on the latest data, the circulation’s reversal began on Tuesday, and computer model guidance expects it to last through Thursday.

Weather patterns take a few weeks to respond to a polar vortex disruption, if at all. Given that reliable forecasts only extend about 10 days into the future, we can’t know where in the northern hemisphere cold air from the Arctic may spill.

While experts are still debating the exact causes driving this polar vortex breakdown, the event throws another wrench into a cool season already dominated by another unprecedented event: the strongest El Niño on record.

Historically warm sea surface temperatures in the eastern Pacific Ocean have already significantly affected conditions around the world, and this influence will only grow heading into the winter months.

Much of North America can expect warmer-than-normal conditions during a winter dominated by a strong El Niño. But every event is different, and now with a sudden disruption in the polar vortex, those forecasts are less certain, because unexpected things can happen when unprecedented phenomena overlap.

"Martian Isolation" is an upcoming single-player, first-person survival horror game that's just been revealed with a suitably creepy launch trailer. And yes, it does look an awful lot like "The Martian," doesn't it?

There's a lot of survival gameplay on display here that mirrors Mark Watney's tale of survival on the Red Planet, as your stranded protagonist is forced to explore the Martian surface to acquire resources, grow plants, and repair their base.

That comparison to Andy Weir's sci-fi masterpiece does fall away as you get further into the trailer, though, when the horror part of the game's description comes into play: Flickering lights, creepy figures stalking the halls of your Martian habitat, and blood dripping from the walls.

Oh yeah, that's some good creepy sci-fi horror right there. It's giving "Event Horizon", and that's always getting a thumbs-up from me.

There's no release date scheduled at this time, with the 'Martian Isolation' Steam page simply listing it as "coming soon," though the YouTube trailer description does say it "will be available on Steam in 2027".

You can't pre-order yet, but if this looks like your jam, you can add it to your wishlist.

Beyond that, we know shockingly little about this title. It's the debut game from Golden Milestone Studio, but there's very little information out there beyond a name. The latest blog post on the game's Steam page says that they're a "small team," but what we've seen so far is encouraging.

There seems to be a pronounced split between the survival and horror elements of the game along the day/night cycle. Daytime sees you exploring the Martian surface, smashing rocks, cleaning solar panels, and doing sick jumps on a quad bike.

The psychological torment only begins once the sun goes down (they mostly come out at night … mostly), as your character starts encountering cosmic horrors and weird naked zombie men.

Are they hallucinations, or is there some malevolent presence hiding in the blood-red sands of Mars?

I'm always looking for new ways to shatter my psyche and possibly soil my pants, so I'll be keeping a close eye on this one. In the meantime, I do need to get back and finish "Routine." I left my character hiding under a desk months ago, and I haven't been brave enough to go back. As Mama always said, you can't have any Martian horror until you finish your lunar horror first.

#655. NASA’s CHAPEA Mars crew finally emerges after more than a year in isolation

After spending more than a year experiencing what life could be like on Mars, four NASA volunteers have finally stepped outside, marking the end of an ambitious experiment designed to prepare humans for future missions to the Red Planet.

The crew completed their simulated Mars journey on October 31, 2026, emerging into the outside world for the first time in more than a year. Although the volunteers never actually left Earth, their extended mission recreated many of the challenges astronauts could encounter while living and working millions of miles from home.

The experiment was part of NASA's Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog (CHAPEA) program, which investigates how people adapt to the demanding conditions of extended space exploration.

The four volunteers were Matthew Montgomery (left), James Spicer (middle left), Ross Elder (middle right), and Ellen Ellis (right). Following the completion of their mission, the crew posed together outdoors, celebrating their return from a simulated journey to another planet.

Throughout the experiment, the participants carried out tasks similar to those that future Mars explorers may need to perform. These included operating and testing essential systems, caring for crops, conserving limited supplies, and conducting extravehicular activities.

Extravehicular activities, often called spacewalks, are operations astronauts perform outside their spacecraft or habitat. In a Mars simulation, these activities help researchers examine how crews might prepare for and carry out work beyond the safety of their living quarters.

The volunteers also had to manage communication delays, an important challenge for anyone traveling to Mars. Unlike astronauts aboard the International Space Station, who can communicate with Earth almost instantly, future Mars explorers will experience significant delays because radio signals take time to cross the enormous distance between the two planets.

These delays mean astronauts cannot always depend on immediate guidance from mission control. They must be prepared to solve problems, make decisions, and manage unexpected situations with greater independence.

One of the biggest challenges of sending people to Mars is keeping them healthy, productive, and safe during long periods away from Earth. A crew must be able to manage food, equipment, living conditions, and daily responsibilities while working together in a confined environment.

NASA uses analog missions to explore these challenges before attempting actual journeys into deep space. An analog mission is a realistic simulation that reproduces selected conditions of space exploration while allowing scientists to study how people respond in a controlled setting on Earth.

The CHAPEA program provides an opportunity to investigate how astronauts might handle the practical demands of extended missions, including resource limitations, equipment maintenance, food production, and communication difficulties.

The lessons learned from Montgomery, Spicer, Elder, and Ellis will help NASA plan future human exploration missions. Their experiences are expected to inform the development of NASA's planned Moon Base and preparations for eventual crewed expeditions to Mars.

Although this crew's journey took place entirely on Earth, the knowledge gained could help address some of the challenges humans will face when they finally travel to the Red Planet.

Every November, I give myself a completely unscientific eyesight test using one of my favorite sights in the night sky — the Pleiades. How many stars can you see?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Every autumn, I conduct an eyesight test that no reputable optometrist would understand.

I go outside, find the Pleiades and count how many stars I can see. Usually I start confidently. One, two, three, four, five. Then things become contentious. Is that another star? Did I actually see it, or did I decide I ought to see it because I know it's there? I look away, look back and begin again.

This is not, I should emphasize, a meaningful test of eye health. What it tests, rather, is how badly I've prepared for looking at the night sky.

The Pleiades sit roughly 444 light-years away in Taurus and are right now becoming extremely convenient in the evening sky. You don't need a telescope to find them. You don't even need binoculars. In fact, you're likely to catch their collective brightness in your peripheral vision every time you go outside and look up.

But every November the Pleiades remind me that naked-eye observing isn't as simple as opening the back door and looking up. How many Pleiades I can see can change depending on what I do during the next 10 minutes.

The Pleiades, also known as Messier 45 (M45) or the "Seven Sisters," are an open star cluster in Taurus. They're one of the closest clusters to the solar system and some of the youngest stars you can see with the naked eye — just 100 million years old. They're basically newborns.

In mid-November, they rise in the east in the early evening and climb higher as the night progresses, making this an excellent time to get acquainted with them. Look east after dark for a tiny, compact group of stars. If you know Orion, which rises later, the Pleiades are above and to the right of it from mid-northern latitudes. Nearby you'll also find orange Aldebaran and the much broader V-shaped Hyades cluster. The Hyades are closer to the sun, but their stars are about 625 million years old.

The name "Seven Sisters" creates an immediate observational trap: people assume they're supposed to see seven stars. That's not necessarily true. In fact, six is a common naked-eye result under decently dark conditions (note that the shape of the six brightest is like a mini Big Dipper/Plough), while people with sharp eyesight under darker skies may see more. The cluster itself contains about 1,000 stars. The number you personally distinguish depends on eyesight, sky brightness, atmospheric conditions and how well your eyes have adapted to darkness.

That makes M45 much more interesting to me than a simple tick-box target. So tonight, don't just find the Pleiades — count them.

I'm going to run my Pleiades eye test in stages. First, I'll step outside and look almost immediately. I'll count the individual stars I can distinguish without spending ages convincing myself about marginal ones. Then I'll wait. After about 10 minutes (without looking at my phone or bright outdoor lights, of course), I'll count again. Full dark adaptation takes considerably longer, but even 10 minutes can make an obvious difference when you've just come from a brightly lit house.

I'll then try my trusty 10x50 binoculars. This is where the experiment stops being subtle. The little naked-eye knot of brightness suddenly becomes a field filled with stars. The Pleiades don't just become brighter through binoculars. Their whole character changes because stars that were below my naked-eye threshold appear. I'll also use the averted vision technique, looking slightly to one side rather than directly at M45. It's one of the best demonstrations of the technique, with its fainter stars seemingly popping into view as your more light-sensitive peripheral vision takes over.

The moon is returning to the evening sky this week, waxing from a thin crescent toward first quarter. It reaches first quarter around Nov. 17, so moonlight becomes progressively more noticeable during the first half of the night. Look southwest during twilight, and you'll see the beautiful sight of a crescent moon sporting Earthshine, sunlight reflected from Earth onto the moon's night side.

Overnight, Nov. 15-16, don't miss Mars and Jupiter in conjunction. The two planets will appear just over a degree apart, rising in the east during the evening before climbing high into the southern sky in the hours before sunrise.

The following night, Nov. 17-18, the Leonid meteor shower peaks. This is one shower where staying up later actually matters. Leo, the constellation containing the shower's radiant, doesn't rise until late, so the better opportunity comes after midnight and toward the predawn hours.

Auriga, "the Charioteer," is easy to see in the northeastern and eastern sky during November evenings, but have you spied the asterism close to its brightest star, Capella? It's known as the "Goat Star," though its Latin name is the diminutive of capra, meaning "little she-goat." The reason is esoteric — Capella represents Amalthea, the mythological goat that suckled the infant Zeus — but there is a neat asterism (shape of stars) nearby that suddenly makes sense. Close to Capella is a triangle of faint stars that are known as The Kids — Epsilon, Zeta and Eta Aurigae — traditionally imagined as the offspring of Capella. It's one of those little patterns that makes a constellation much easier to recognize.

He is the editor of WhenIsTheNextEclipse.com, author of A Stargazing Program For Beginners, co-author of The Eclipse Effect, and a senior contributor at Forbes.

#652. 237-million-year-old fossils reveal a bizarre armored sea amphibian

A remarkable fossil discovery in China has revealed an ancient amphibian that lived entirely in the ocean, something no amphibian alive today is known to do. The unusual animal, named Gerrothorax maritimus, had a broad, flattened body protected by bony armor and was roughly the size of a giant salamander. Researchers believe it spent much of its life on the seafloor, waiting to ambush passing prey.

The discovery comes from an international team at the University of California, Davis, Peking University, and the Geological Museum of Guizhou. Their findings, published in Nature Ecology & Evolution, are based on two exceptionally well-preserved skeletons dating back nearly 237 million years to the Late Triassic period.

Both fossils were uncovered in China's Guizhou Province, in a region that was once submerged beneath an ancient ocean hundreds of miles from major landmasses.

"This area is part of an ecosystem that we've been looking at and trying to reconstruct," said study corresponding author Ryosuke Motani, a professor in the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences at UC Davis. "We've been mostly studying marine reptiles and the fish from this place, but now we also have this amphibian, and it's a sort of very unusual member of the lineage."

The finding is especially surprising because amphibians are generally unable to survive in seawater. Among the more than 8,000 amphibian species living today, none are known to spend their entire lives in marine environments, and fewer than 2% have any ability to tolerate salt.

Mammals, reptiles, and birds, by comparison, all include species that can live entirely at sea without relying on land for food or fresh water. Until this discovery, scientists had never identified convincing fossil evidence of an amphibian with the same ability.

A Giant Armored Amphibian Built for the Seafloor

Because the two skeletons are so complete, researchers were able to piece together the animal's appearance and develop a clearer picture of how it lived.

Gerrothorax maritimus measured nearly three feet long, but its proportions were far different from those of a modern salamander. Rather than having a long, slender body, it was unusually broad and flattened, with a distinctive disc-shaped form.

Its body was also covered in thick bony armor, which may have helped protect it from large marine predators such as ichthyosaurs.

"If you think about today's amphibians, this animal is unusual because it's big," Motani said. "It's probably, body mass-wise, about the same as the giant salamander, but what's different is that giant salamanders are elongated whereas this animal is really chunky."

The structure of its skull, together with its heavy armor, suggests that this ancient amphibian was an ambush predator. Instead of actively chasing its meals, it likely rested on the seafloor until an unsuspecting animal came within reach.

"They would probably just wait at the bottom and then when prey comes around, they would just suck it in," said Motani, who noted that the hunting strategy resembles that of the wobbegong, a type of carpet shark that lives near the seafloor and captures prey using suction.

How Could an Amphibian Survive in Salt Water?

One of the biggest mysteries surrounding Gerrothorax maritimus is how it managed to survive in an environment that is hostile to nearly all modern amphibians.

The problem comes down largely to amphibian skin. Unlike the relatively waterproof skin of many other animals, amphibian skin allows water and gases to pass through it. This makes it useful for breathing and maintaining hydration, but also leaves amphibians especially vulnerable to the effects of salt water.

"That skin is permeable, and that allows the animals to use it for multiple purposes," said Motani. "They use it for respiration and water intake, so amphibians don't drink or breathe through the mouth because they can do both through the skin."

As a result, modern amphibians generally depend on freshwater habitats or environments close to them. A few species have developed limited salt tolerance, including the crab-eating frog. Even these animals can lose weight when exposed to brackish water and must eventually return to freshwater to recover.

The ancient Gerrothorax maritimus, however, may have evolved a very different solution.

Researchers suggest that its extensive bony armor restricted the movement of water through its skin. This protective covering may have reduced its dependence on absorbing water directly through the skin, allowing the animal to take in seawater through its mouth instead.

Under this proposed mechanism, water would have been absorbed through the digestive tract, while the animal's gills could have helped eliminate excess salt. Gills are known to have been present in members of the Gerrothorax genus, giving the researchers reason to suspect that this species possessed a more fishlike approach to managing its salt balance.

Together, these adaptations may explain how an amphibian managed to occupy an ecological niche that remains inaccessible to its modern relatives.

Fossil Evidence Points to a Fully Marine Lifestyle

The researchers also examined whether Gerrothorax maritimus truly lived in the ocean or whether its remains might have been transported there after death.

Several clues strongly favor a marine lifestyle.

First, the skeletons were recovered from sediments deposited in a deep marine environment. Their remarkable completeness also provides important evidence about where the animals died.

"Carcasses at sea, unless they sink to the bottom right away, tend to dry out and lose limbs prior to sinking to the bottom," said Motani. "But these animals had their fingers preserved, so that means they probably died near where they lived."

The preservation of such delicate skeletal structures suggests that the bodies were not carried long distances before reaching the seafloor.

To investigate further, the team analyzed the fossils' chemical composition, focusing on the relative abundance of different forms of strontium, known as isotopes.

The results closely matched the strontium isotope signatures expected in ocean water during the Late Triassic, providing another independent line of evidence that the animals inhabited a marine environment.

Taken together, the fossil preservation, geological setting, and chemical findings make a compelling case that Gerrothorax maritimus spent its life entirely at sea.

The discovery reveals an unexpected evolutionary path for amphibians, showing that at least one ancient species appears to have overcome the biological limitations that keep its living relatives largely confined to freshwater environments.

The research received funding from the National Natural Science Foundation of China.

#651. Rocco Classic Smart Fridge Review: A Cool Conversation Piece

Updated November 2026: The Rocco Super Smart Fridge is now called the Rocco Classic, after Rocco released two new fridges in 2026, the lower-priced Essential and desktop-sized Mini Mini. Copy has been updated to reflect the new moniker.

Opening up someone else’s kitchen refrigerator is an intimate act.

I for one would prefer my guests don’t go in there for a beer and see the raspberries that are probably moldy, revealing a dark side of my personality. I’ll just get their drink for them. Having a separate mini fridge just for drinks can help, and when I saw how fresh and innovative the Rocco seemed, I had to know more.

The Rocco Classic feels more like a piece of furniture sitting in my living room, as opposed to a regular mini fridge, which often looks like it’s out of a college dorm, or a more industrial-looking regular wine fridge. I have the matte graphite color (it also comes in white, green, brown, and mirror-black).

The whole thing is mostly made of steel, which makes it strong and heavy, and the rounded edges give it more of a soft appeal. It seems to be engineered very well, with quality materials, which I’m sure is why it costs as much as it does. This should last me a very long time in my home. Overall, it’s a beautiful statement piece that people who like to host in their home will love, but the features that make this a smart fridge are not perfect.

A typical wine fridge will generally fit full-size bottles of wine only, but the Classic can fit 77 12-ounce cans (though Rocco's website says 88) or 27 wine bottles in its 34.5 x 24 x 16-inch body (H x W x D). There are six shelves, each of which is designed so you can store bottles and cans of any size and stagger them to fit like a puzzle. Each shelf is also reversible so the grooves match whichever shape bottles you choose to place on each shelf.

The Rocco connects to an app on your phone (currently available only for iOS; Rocco hopes to have an Android version at some point). The app is simple and easy to use, but there aren’t that many things to do on it, and some of the features feel forced. First of all, there are a few modes you can control from the app. I keep mine on Quiet Mode. It really is extremely quiet. I rarely hear much of a rumbling noise from the compressor compared to other fridges.

Similarly, there’s Smart Mode, which makes it work more like a thermostat when the fridge is sitting in a warmer temperature. There’s also Party Mode, which prioritizes keeping the drinks cold more so than making less noise. After a few minutes, I did hear the compressor get a little louder. I opened it a few minutes later, and it was definitely colder in there. (Rocco gives the temperature range as 37 to 64 degrees Fahrenheit.)

But if I want the drinks to stay colder while I’m having a party where people are opening it often, I could just lower the temperature to where I want it myself. I really don’t see much of a need for all of these modes. Using a wireless Bluetooth thermometer, I tested the temperature changes inside the fridge for each mode to make sure they work properly. I gave each of them 10 minutes to change and tested each shelf on both ends of the fridge. I was pleased to find these were all within just a few degrees difference of what the fridge read.

The other primary feature of the app is the vision system. When you first set up the app, sensors in the fridge scan everything you’re storing in it. Every beverage then shows up on your app, organized by drawer. I’m storing some pretty obscure drinks, like OoMee algae-infused beverage and Yaté yerba mate, and it recognized most of them, so I was impressed, although some, like my Dolin vermouth, which is one of the most popular vermouth brands, were not recognized.

Nutrition facts also pop up for each drink, although many of them are incomplete. In theory, you could go to the grocery store and see which drinks you’re running low on just by looking at the app. I found that I didn’t do this much, although I was curious if I was running low on LaCroix once and checked the app to see that I certainly was. So it came in handy.

However, the system is not perfect. Right now it’s showing that I still have one LaCroix remaining, although I haven’t had one in there in a couple of weeks. I would love it if I could purchase something I’m running low on directly from the app.

The dual-temperature system also allows you to make half of the fridge one temperature and the other half another, which you can adjust manually or through the app. While this is important so that I can keep seltzers and wines at different temperatures, this is the one feature that’s on many wine fridges, so it’s not unique to the Classic.

The Classic has a kind of mid-century vibe but also feels contemporary. I love the fluted glass door, which looks stunning when it’s nighttime and the lights inside are peeking through it. Any time someone comes to my apartment it becomes a topic of conversation. You can turn the light on and off and adjust the brightness from the app.

The top surface of the fridge is flat and sturdy, so it doubles as a bar cart. The raised lip on the sides also helps so that bottles I’m placing on it have less of a chance of falling off. I have a bar cart that’s overflowing with bottles, so it’s nice to have this right next to it for some overflow.

As someone who loves to make a nightly martini, I’ve hated having to go to my kitchen fridge for the vermouth. Now I store my vermouth right in my Rocco and I don’t have to break up my rhythm as much (other than grabbing ice and the chilled glass from the kitchen freezer). The Classic also comes with a pack of round playing cards that double as coasters. They’re a little flimsy for coasters, but it’s a cute touch.

The fridge beeps when the door doesn’t shut all the way. It’s a pretty soft beep—I didn’t hear it over the TV playing. I wish I got a push notification when the door wasn’t shut. That would have been a much better use of the app. You really have to make sure the door is all the way shut, because it’s not soft-close, nor are the drawers, which I wish were. The small bottom drawer on mine is also a little bit stubborn to pull out and close, although all the other doors slide nice and smoothly.

The price does make your heart skip a beat. But that aligns with other higher-end wine fridges on the market. You also don't need to worry about installing this fridge into your cabinetry, as it’s a stand-alone piece. The precision and engineering of this fridge make the price seem reasonable when compared with others, and it actually has character, whereas just about every other wine fridge looks the same.

Additionally, the price includes a 10-year warranty. For an additional fee, you can get white glove delivery, where it’s placed in your home exactly where you want it and the packaging is removed for you. This is probably not worth it. Otherwise, shipping is free.

The Rocco makes your living room more of an active social space by keeping your guests in the same cozy area. It’s furniture, which I wouldn’t say about most other fridges. I think people are going to buy this fridge more because of the way it looks rather than the fact that it’s a smart fridge. I’m a beverage enthusiast, so I love having the Rocco to show for it.

#649. NASA’s Parker Solar Probe discovers a hidden pattern in the Sun’s chaotic magnetic fields

Turbulence is all around us, from milk swirling into a cup of coffee to powerful storms churning through the atmosphere and oceans. But turbulence also occurs throughout space, where it behaves in ways that scientists are still struggling to understand.

Unlike the air and water on Earth, much of the matter in space consists of electrically charged particles in a state (known as the plasma state). These particles interact strongly with magnetic and electric fields, creating turbulence that is fundamentally different from what we experience on Earth. Space plasma is also so thinly spread that particles rarely collide with one another, making its behavior even more unusual.

Scientists have long struggled to explain how turbulence develops under these conditions and how energy is distributed among its constantly changing fluctuations. Now, an international research team has uncovered a surprising clue: hidden within the seemingly random motion of space plasma is a distinct magnetic pattern that reverses direction at very small scales.

The discovery, published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, reveals a previously unobserved phenomenon that could improve our understanding of the solar wind and the turbulent conditions that influence space weather.

NASA's Parker Solar Probe Reveals a Hidden Magnetic Reversal

Researchers from the Technische Universität Braunschweig and the University of Tokyo, working with Tohoku University, Kyushu University, Osaka University, and other international institutions, identified the phenomenon using observations from NASA's Parker Solar Probe.

The collaboration brought together scientists from ten countries, including researchers at the Institute of Theoretical Physics at Technische Universität Braunschweig.

By analyzing highly precise measurements of magnetic fields and particles, the team discovered that turbulent magnetic fields reverse their direction of rotation at a particular range of wavelengths. This marks the first direct observation of such a reversal in space turbulence.

Even more surprisingly, the reversal becomes more pronounced and shifts toward longer wavelengths as the solar wind travels farther from the Sun.

The change occurs at a critical boundary where the behavior of plasma shifts from the collective movement of a flowing fluid to the dynamics of individual particles. This connection suggests that the magnetic reversal may provide an important new way to understand how turbulence operates across different physical scales.

Finding Order in the Chaos of Space Turbulence

At larger scales, plasma moves much like a fluid. Swirling structures called vortices and electromagnetic waves create increasingly complex fluctuations, producing the turbulent conditions found throughout space.

Although these movements appear random, the researchers discovered that the rotation of the magnetic fields follows a consistent pattern.

When viewed along a direction pointing outward from the Sun, magnetic fields at larger scales tend to rotate counterclockwise. At much smaller scales, however, the preferred rotation switches to clockwise.

This reversal occurs precisely where plasma stops behaving primarily like a fluid and begins exhibiting behavior governed by individual particles.

The finding is particularly striking because it reveals a clear, organized feature within a system otherwise dominated by seemingly unpredictable fluctuations.

"We see a clear structure in the spectrum, even though the turbulence represents unstructured motions," says Dr. Masatomi Iizawa (TU Braunschweig), the study's first author.

Dr. Yokoi (University. of Tokyo) emphasizes the broader importance of the discovery, stating, "The results are of great significance for both plasma physics and astrophysics."

Why the Discovery Matters for Solar Storms and Space Weather

Although the magnetic reversal occurs at extremely small scales, understanding it could have far-reaching consequences for space physics.

Plasma turbulence is a major feature of many environments throughout the universe, including Earth's magnetosphere, the solar wind, regions affected by solar eruptions, interplanetary space, and the disks of material surrounding astronomical objects known as accretion disks.

It also influences the shock waves and clouds of magnetic material that travel through interplanetary space following eruptions on the Sun.

These disturbances can play an important role in geomagnetic storms, making plasma turbulence a critical factor in efforts to predict space weather.

By showing how an organized magnetic pattern emerges as turbulent plasma transitions from fluid behavior to particle behavior, the new research provides an important piece of a longstanding physics puzzle. The findings could ultimately help scientists better understand the complex processes that govern the solar wind and improve the physical models used to forecast geomagnetic storms.

LOS ANGELES — The California Science Center officially opened its brand-new Samuel Oschin Air & Space Center to the public today (Nov. 13).

After more than three decades in development, folks can finally visit the Los Angeles science museum's massive new wing. For most of us, the biggest draw is its centerpiece: the retired space shuttle Endeavour, sitting upright in launch position, towering at nearly 200 feet (61 meters) tall.

"It just takes your breath away when you see that reveal and the doors open and you get to look at it for the first time. It's just — it's overwhelming," former NASA astronaut Garrett Reisman told Space.com during a visit to the museum. Reisman flew on two space shuttle missions during his astronaut career, the first of which was on Endeavour.

"There are people that come from all over the world, and when they come to Los Angeles, they're going to have the opportunity to see it, too," Reisman added. "The exposure it's going to have is just a force multiplier. There are so many people that can have that opportunity to bring their kids here and show them [the shuttle] and have that experience."

Entering into this exhibit is an experience in and of itself, as I can personally attest; I was among of group of reporters who got a sneak peek at the new wing on Oct. 28. A video presentation ends in a dramatic reveal: Visitors walk into a space where the enormous shuttle, which flew 25 missions to Earth orbit from 1992 to 2011, feels truly larger than life.

There are a number of interactive exhibits around the base of Endeavour, which you can slide down to (though, of course, you can also take the elevator or stairs). From a shuttle landing simulator to a replica of a shuttle cockpit that you can sit in, to shuttle tires and space tech from across decades of spaceflight history, there's an incredible variety of space artifacts to both observe and interact with.

As for Endeavour itself: It is open, so you can peer inside to see the robotic arm tucked away among a myriad of handles, straps and electronic gear inside. And you can see the shuttle from underneath all the way to the top.

You can lie on the floor underneath the shuttle's engines, for example, and then take an elevator up the launch tower to come face-to-face with Endeavour's nose. There's even a transparent floor at the top that allows you to stand above the shuttle (though if you have a fear of heights, this might not be for you).

This is the abbreviated description, but know that if you are visiting the California Science Center, you will want to budget a serious amount of time to explore all that this new center has to offer.

The new air and space center is designed for all ages, and for civilians and astronauts alike. For instance, looking at Endeavour spurred some memories for Reisman: He reflected on his time aboard the shuttle and his time as an astronaut and pinpointed specific places on the shuttle that played important roles in his mission.

"I'm looking at handrails that I held onto during a spacewalk," he said. "They're the same handrails. My hand was in the glove, but it was wrapped around those handrails. And I practiced for a long time exactly how I was going to do that, how I was going to root my tether, and all that kind of stuff. And I get to stand [here] now. When you go up the elevator there, you can actually have a direct view of those handrails, and every time I see that, I'm thinking about that spacewalk."

But you don't need to have completed a spacewalk to get that view. And, as of today, the general public is welcome to visit the museum, which is free to the public — as is the new aerospace center with its Endeavour exhibit.

However, due to the excitement over this new center opening, you will need to make a reservation online to attend. And, while the museum is free to the public, there is a cost associated with reserving slots during these busy first few days.

Chelsea Gohd served as a Senior Writer for Space.com from 2018 to 2022 before returning in 2026, covering everything from climate change to planetary science and human spaceflight in both articles and on-camera in videos. With a M.S. in Biology, Chelsea has written and worked for institutions including NASA JPL, the American Museum of Natural History, Scientific American, Discover Magazine Blog, Astronomy Magazine, and Live Science. When not writing, editing or filming something space-y, Gohd is writing music and performing as Foxanne, even launching a song to space in 2021 with Inspiration4. #647. The mystery of how hair knows where to grow may finally be solved

Long before a mammal is born, its skin begins establishing the precise locations where hair will eventually grow. These developing hair follicles form intricate geometric arrangements that differ from species to species. But what determines where each follicle appears, and how does the body create such orderly patterns?

Researchers at the University of Geneva (UNIGE) have identified a surprisingly simple process that may help explain this biological mystery. By studying how cells move in response to chemical signals, the team developed a model that successfully recreates the formation of hair follicle patterns in two mammalian species. Their findings, published in PNAS, suggest that elaborate biological structures can emerge naturally from basic interactions between neighboring cells.

The discovery could help explain a much broader phenomenon in nature. Hair, feathers, and most types of scales begin as small structures called placodes that appear during embryonic development. Scientists have spent decades investigating how these early structures establish the distinctive arrangements seen across different animal species.

Challenging a Long-Standing Theory of Hair Growth

For laboratory mice (Mus musculus), the leading explanation has traditionally been the expansion-induction model. This theory proposes that when a new placode appears, it releases a chemical that prevents additional placodes from developing too close to it.

As the embryo's skin grows and stretches, some areas move far enough away from existing placodes to escape the chemical's influence. New placodes can then develop in those spaces, gradually creating a more complete pattern across the skin.

Although this explanation has gained widespread acceptance, scientists have not experimentally established that it can account for the diversity of follicle patterns found across species.

A Simpler Mechanism for Hair Follicle Formation

To investigate another possibility, researchers led by Athanasia Tzika, Senior Lecturer, and Michel Milinkovitch, Professor, both in the Department of Genetics and Evolution at UNIGE's Faculty of Science, focused on a process called chemotaxis.

Chemotaxis occurs when cells move in response to differences in chemical concentrations. The same basic process helps guide white blood cells toward areas of inflammation, allowing the immune system to respond where it is needed.

The researchers created a mathematical model that tracks how mobile cells in the dermis interact with an attracting chemical signal released by the epidermis, the skin's outer layer. They then simulated the growth of embryonic skin to see whether these interactions could produce the gradual appearance of placodes.

Remarkably, the model recreated the developmental patterns observed in laboratory mice, including the same sequence of follicle formation that scientists had previously explained using the expansion-induction theory. This suggests that a complex system of instructions may not be necessary to determine where follicles develop.

"Our findings show that the observed patterns do not require a complex system telling each placode where to form," explain Muhamet Ibrahimi and Ebrahim Jahanbakhsh, researchers in the Department of Genetics and Evolution. "Instead, placodes emerge spontaneously from local interactions between cells and chemical signals."

One Simple Process Creates Different Hair Patterns

The team next investigated whether the same mechanism could explain follicle arrangements in another mammal with a very different coat structure.

They selected the spiny mouse (Acomys dimidiatus), a rodent whose hair follicles develop in an unusually regular pattern with a strong directional alignment. This distinctive organization cannot be explained by the traditional expansion-induction model.

Using experimental information gathered from three-dimensional images of developing embryonic skin, the researchers adapted their simulations to reflect the spiny mouse's particular biochemical characteristics and the way its skin grows.

The results showed that the same underlying process of cells responding to chemical signals could also reproduce the spiny mouse's highly organized follicle pattern. The differences between the two species could be explained by variations in their cellular interactions, chemical properties, and skin growth rather than entirely different mechanisms.

These findings suggest that the remarkable variety of structures found throughout the animal kingdom may arise from a shared set of relatively simple biological rules. By adjusting how cells interact and respond to their surroundings, nature can generate dramatically different patterns without requiring a separate developmental blueprint for every species.

"Our work suggests that simple cellular interactions can generate the remarkable diversity of tissue architectures observed throughout evolution," concludes Athanasia Tzika. "The differences observed between species therefore result from the same self-organization process, but with variations in the interactions between cells and chemical signals."

#645. Google Wanted Spirit Airlines Data. Flight Attendants Found a Way to Opt Out

An agreement reached this week between Google and a union representing an unlikely workforce—flight attendants—could reveal a more permanent answer by creating a process that might reliably separate the data that workers produce from their own personal information. A judge still needs to approve the agreement next week.

The revised deal requires Spirit to hire a third-party data de-identification company, called Tonic AI, to exclude information that could potentially be associated with individual consumers or employees. Tonic will also be charged with ensuring that data, once de-identified, cannot be relinked to specific people. Google has promised to maintain the data in this new, de-identified form.

Many sensitive records will be excluded from the sale, including employee medical records, documents related to employee investigations and labor relations, and information about industry-wide safety management systems. In early November, a trade organization representing airlines chimed in on the sale, arguing that including that information could make employees less willing to come forward to report safety issues through voluntary programs, which are widely regarded as critical to the US aviation industry’s strong safety record.

The proposed agreement also includes an opt-out clause. Google can choose to renege on the sale if the data-cleaning process reduces the assets by more than 8 percent. Google didn’t respond to a request for comment.

Association for Flight Attendants president Sara Nelson tells WIRED she’s as surprised as anyone that flight attendants are at the forefront of AI-related workers’ rights issues, which often focus on employees who, willingly or unwillingly, train their machine replacements.

“It’s very hard to replace a flight attendant—you’d need a high-functioning robot, and that seems to be further off,” she says. “What this shows is that this is an issue even in jobs you think are most protected from AI. This is an issue for everyone.”

She said the union will immediately begin to demand that other airlines include worker-data-protection clauses in their labor agreements. “If you’re not willing to meet these standards for your workers, we’re going to shame you,” she says. The Association for Flight Attendants has begun meeting with state-level politicians to craft legislation that would write worker data protections into law.

Tech leaders have argued that workers understand that their information will train AI models, which will ultimately make their lives better and easier. “You have to think of the upside, the abundance that AI can result in,” one executive told WIRED this month.

Nelson says US workers aren’t buying the upside of AI and that they’re part of the wider electorate that seems to be growing warier of the tech by the day. She says the vision of AI abundance is “a fantasyland of people in boardrooms with beanbags who wear hoodies.”

Liftoff is scheduled for 12:30 a.m. ET on Saturday (Nov. 14).

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Rocket Lab will launch its 100th space mission early Saturday morning (Nov. 14), and you can watch the milestone liftoff live.

An Electron rocket topped with a private Japanese Earth-observing satellite is scheduled to launch from Rocket Lab's New Zealand site on Saturday, during a window that opens at 12:30 a.m. EST (0530 GMT; 6:30 p.m. local time).

The mission, which Rocket Lab calls "The Mountain God Rises," will be the 100th to date for the California-based company. You can watch it live via Rocket Lab here, and Space.com will carry the feed if, as expected, it's made available. Coverage will begin about 30 minutes before launch.

Rocket Lab launched for the first time in May 2017, sending the brand-new Electron up on a test flight from New Zealand. That effort failed, but Electron bounced back on its second-ever liftoff, delivering several cubesats to low Earth orbit (LEO) in January 2018.

In the years since, the 59-foot-tall (18 meters) Electron has become one of the most prolific and reliable rockets in the world, carrying small payloads to the final frontier for a variety of customers.

And it's hitting the century mark in record-breaking fashion: No commercially developed rocket has gotten there faster, not even SpaceX's workhorse Falcon 9, according to Rocket Lab founder and CEO Peter Beck.

"It's an unprecedented milestone for a commercial small-lift orbital rocket, and a threshold rarely crossed in modern spaceflight," Beck said on Monday (Nov. 9), during Rocket Lab's third-quarter earnings call with investors. "But what matters most to us and our customers is that we have achieved a 96% reliability rate across 99 launches."

Electron will meet the moment in style on Saturday morning, thanks to some fancy livery.

"Black rocket 🤝 Golden milestone. Electron is all dressed up for launch 100," Rocket Lab said via X on Tuesday (Nov. 10), in a post that shared a photo of the specially painted first stage.

Not all of Rocket Lab's missions have gone orbital, it should be noted: A suborbital variant of Electron known as HASTE, which customers use to test technologies in a hypersonic flight environment, has nine missions under its belt to date.

"The Mountain God Rises" will be Rocket Lab's 11th launch to date for the Tokyo-based company iQPS, which is building a constellation of three dozen synthetic aperture radar (SAR) satellites in LEO. If all goes to plan, Electron's upper "kick stage" will deploy a single iQPS spacecraft 357 miles (575 kilometers) above Earth.

SAR satellites can see through cloud cover and image our planet at night as well as during the day, offering key advantages over spacecraft that are optimized to view in optical wavelengths.

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz.
